The paper uses darker/larger regions to argue more global and more semantically aligned dependency capture, yet there is no quantitative correlation shown between ERF properties and actual coding gain. In other words, the figures are suggestive, not dispositive. The authors should be more careful not to oversell them.

There are several presentation-level inaccuracies and notation slips that reduce confidence. In Section 3.1 on Page 3, the paper states that the analysis transform $g_a$ encodes an input image into latent features $\mathbf{y}=g_s(\mathbf{x};\theta_s)$, which is clearly inconsistent and appears to swap $g_a$ and $g_s$. The rate term is also written at scalar level as $p_{\hat y}(\hat y \mid \mu,\sigma,\varphi)$ rather than more consistently in vectorized latent notation. None of these alone is fatal, but together they create friction in a paper whose main selling point depends on custom architecture equations being precisely understood.

The contribution to entropy modeling appears limited, and the main paper admits as much. On Page 8, the authors state that adding CAM to the entropy model yields negligible gains while increasing latency. This is honest, but it also means the proposed architectural idea is narrower than the paper’s framing around “content-aware Mamba for learned image compression” might imply. In practice, most of the gain seems to come from improving transform networks, not from a broader rethinking of the full codec pipeline.

The mathematical formulation of the FF model is unclear and in places internally inconsistent. The core definition in Equation (1) writes g^l = ||h^l||_1, but immediately states g^l is a J-dimensional goodness vector. A plain L1 norm is a scalar, not a class-wise vector, leaving the objective underspecified.

Algorithm 1 and the corresponding equations are not mathematically well specified enough to reproduce or verify the method. Gradients are not written explicitly with respect to parameters, and it is not specified whether z_g^{l-1} is computed independently or if gradients stop through g_*^l as constants.

The training objective for unlearning is heuristic and lacks justification relative to the stated problem formulation in Equation (4). The paper does not explain why matching the guidance model's goodness distribution on forgetting samples is the right surrogate for unlearning or in what sense it approximates retraining on D_remain.

The experimental comparison is too narrow for the strength of the claims. The main text compares primarily against retraining and direct gradient ascent, but should compare in the main text against stronger approximate unlearning families, especially teacher-student or distillation-style methods.

The evaluation protocol for unlearning effectiveness is not fully convincing, and some metrics are interpreted too optimistically. Arguing that similar accuracy on D_forget and D_test implies effective unlearning is a rough heuristic, not a reliable criterion, as it does not imply the removed points no longer have special influence.

The gains over retraining are meaningful but not overwhelming once guidance-model cost is included, and the presentation around efficiency is slightly slippery. A notable fraction of the savings comes from using partial-data or partial-epoch guidance models, which degrades unlearning quality, making it a trade-off rather than a free lunch.

The claims about G-MIA being a 'strict black-box' method are overstated given the access assumptions. The attacker is assumed to obtain layer-wise goodness vectors from all layers, which is stronger than merely observing the final prediction API and not the generic black-box setting readers may infer.

The empirical support for G-MIA is somewhat incomplete in the main paper. The main paper omits AUC despite introducing it as a metric, and the richer analysis of attack input dimensionality appears only in the appendix, making the main-paper evidence suggestive but not definitive.

Presentation quality is uneven, with several notation and writing issues that make an already specialized paper harder to trust. Examples include a typo in the definition of z^l, a malformed phrase 'collect the goodness vector g_i x;theta', and a confusing comparison in Section 6.2.

The literature positioning is incomplete in one relevant direction. The related work does not engage with layer-wise or layer-targeted unlearning ideas that are conceptually close to what this paper advocates, making the contribution appear more isolated than it actually is.

The treatment of constraints in the theorem statements is inconsistent, and in one place incorrect. In Theorem 1, the full-participation result claims (ii) g(w_bar) - g(w*) <= epsilon, but for a constrained problem of the form g(w) <= 0, the natural feasibility statement is g(w_bar) <= epsilon, not a bound relative to g(w*). Since g(w*) need not be zero, the theorem as written is not the same guarantee.

The role of the feasible set X is contradictory across the paper. The main problem is posed over w in X, and Algorithm 1 updates local models by plain gradient steps with no projection in the local loop. Yet the appendix theorems repeatedly switch assumptions between X being a compact convex subset of R^d and X=R^d, and Theorem 4 uses projected global updates. These are materially different algorithms, and the reader is left to guess which setting the main claims actually cover.

Algorithm 1 is underspecified and, in places, wrong at the level of notation. The gradients are missing evaluation points, and the actual pseudocode shown in the main paper does not include the compression/error-feedback steps at all. For a paper whose title explicitly emphasizes 'bidirectionally compressed' optimization, this is a serious omission in the main text.

There are visible inconsistencies between main-text theorem constants and appendix theorem constants. The Gamma expressions in Theorem 1, Theorem 3, and Theorem 6 use different decompositions that do not match cleanly, and Theorem 2 displays a malformed Gamma expression which is mathematically nonsensical as written.

The partial-participation concentration term is suspiciously inconsistent in the exposition. On Page 6, the discussion states that the concentration radius scales like 1/m, not 1/sqrt(m). Under Assumption 4, the natural deviation scale is O(sigma/sqrt(m)), which is what later lemmas use. If the main interpretation paragraph gets the scaling wrong, it is hard to fully trust the theorem presentation.

Some proofs contain concrete mathematical mistakes or at least careless substitutions that change the object being bounded. For instance, in Lemma 1, the second case for t in B writes TermA using the gradient of f_j even though the update in B is supposed to use the gradient of g_j. This copy-paste mistake matters in a switching method.

The claimed connection to prior work is overstated, and the novelty positioning is not fully convincing from the main paper. The paper repeatedly says this is the first unified framework for constraints, compression, local updates, and partial participation, but the appendix references very closely related switching-gradient work, suggesting parts of the contribution are extensions of known ingredients rather than a fundamentally new optimization principle.

The experimental evidence is thinner than the breadth of the claims. The core theory is for convex constrained optimization, but the experimental section gives one small logistic-regression NP classification example and one non-convex RL example. The NP task is based on a very mild federated setting that does not really stress heterogeneity, and the RL experiment does not test the convex theory at all.

The experimental baseline selection is weak in the main paper. There is essentially no direct comparison against constrained FL baselines, primal-dual methods, or even a carefully tuned penalty-based approach in the core pages. Given the paper's very strong claims about avoiding penalty tuning and outperforming practical alternatives, this omission matters.

The interpretation of the figures is somewhat selective and sometimes weaker than the text suggests. In Figure 2, the top row suggests fairly noticeable instability in the constraint curves even under soft switching for larger E. Similarly, Figure 3 for CMDP does not convincingly show a clean dominance pattern; the trajectories are noisy, and the reward advantage of one variant over another is not stable enough to support strong claims.

Table 1 raises questions that the text does not really answer. Top-K with K/d=0.5 reaches only reward 131.6 after 500 rounds, far below the no-compression and quantized variants, and K/d=0.25 barely learns at all. That is a major degradation, yet the surrounding discussion frames the results mostly as evidence that the method 'stably satisfies constraints and maximizes episodic reward,' which is too broad given the table.

Presentation quality is noticeably below the standard expected for a theory-heavy ICLR paper. Beyond local typos, there are malformed formulas, duplicated or broken references, and apparent document corruption on Pages 11-12, where unrelated-looking figures and text fragments appear. A paper asking reviewers to trust a long technical appendix needs much tighter presentation than this.

The main text leaves important implementation details to the appendix while still making strong practical claims. For example, the exact bidirectional EF update, residual handling, and compressor simulation details are not clear enough from the main algorithm. In Table 1, Top-K and quantization are 'simulated' in a simplified way rather than being implemented as actual datatype conversion or bandwidth-constrained transmission, which weakens the practical interpretation of the communication-efficiency claims.

The soft-switching theorem is incomplete relative to the overall framework claim. Theorem 2 in the main paper only addresses full participation. The abstract and title present a unified framework spanning partial participation as well, but the soft-switching guarantees under partial participation are not established in the main text.

The paper’s central “systematic benchmark” claim is undermined by the lack of strong task-specific baselines. The experiments do not include any specialized methods (such as Debin, StateFormer, Osprey, ReSym) as baselines, making it difficult to judge whether the observed failure is due to the tasks being intrinsically hard, the prompt setup being weak, or the chosen models being inappropriate.

The main contribution is closer to an engineering benchmark than a scientific study, and the paper overstates novelty by claiming to conduct the “first systematic, large-scale evaluation” when the actual novelty is limited to evaluating existing models with a prompting and post-processing pipeline without new models, learning objectives, theoretical insights, or evaluation principles.

The evaluation protocol for name recovery is underspecified because the paper never mathematically defines how partial semantic similarity scores are converted into precision, recall, and F1 at the sample or corpus level, including how predicted identifiers are matched to gold identifiers.

The use of an auxiliary LLM for response extraction introduces a second model into the evaluation loop, but its reliability is not validated (e.g., no quantitative validation such as agreement with manual extraction, error rates, or examples where parser decisions change scores).

There is substantial ambiguity about what exactly is being predicted for name recovery, especially for functions with multiple callees. The paper does not cleanly formalize whether the target is a set of all callee names plus the enclosing function name, if order matters, how duplicates are handled, or how cardinality mismatch is scored.

The fine-tuning setup is far too thinly specified for a paper that draws conclusions about the benefit of fine-tuning. The main paper lacks details on LoRA rank, target modules, learning rate, batch size, number of epochs, sequence length, optimizer, scheduler, checkpoint selection rule, and whether all models used matched budgets.

The interpretation of results is often overconfident relative to the evidence. For example, claiming 'training data quality is a more decisive factor' and 'training quality significantly impacts performance' is not established because the compared models differ in many ways beyond data quality. Likewise, Figure 2 does not justify a broad claim about model size being generally unimportant.

The paper’s own tables raise unanswered questions that are not analyzed. For instance, in Table 3, some fine-tuned variable-name recovery results improve dramatically at O0 but collapse at other optimization levels, and in Table 4, some fine-tuned type inference results become exactly 0.00. The analysis merely says improvements are 'inconsistent' without explaining these anomalies.

The x86-64 centric presentation weakens the “large-scale” claim in the main narrative. The main conclusions are written in a way that sounds universal, but extra architecture tables show nontrivial variation across x86-32, ARM, and MIPS (e.g., variable-name recovery on ARM is materially higher after fine-tuning than x86-64). The paper should discuss this rather than collapsing it into 'similar trends'.

The real-world firmware experiment is too underdescribed to carry much weight. Table 6 reports near-zero F1 but the paper does not specify the number of firmware binaries, domains, labeling procedure, symbol provenance, architecture mix, or whether the dataset overlaps with the training/evaluation distribution.

There are consistency and presentation issues that make the experimental story harder to trust. Table 1 says 'nine' LLMs while Section 4.2 says 'eight'; the paper alternates between 'Deepseek-R1' and 'DeepSeek-R1', 'decompiled/decomplied/decomposed', and 'decompilers/decompliers'; and Table 4 says 'x64' while elsewhere it uses 'x86-64'.

Figure 1 indirectly reveals how dependent the conclusions are on a semantic scoring choice that is not formally specified. This should have prompted a sensitivity analysis, not just a one-line takeaway.

Figure 2 jumps from '34B does not beat 7B' to 'training quality is more important than parameter count,' which is not demonstrated by this figure. The figure only supports a local empirical observation under one family and one prompting/evaluation setup, nothing more.

The task setup may unintentionally strip away information in a way that makes the benchmark less representative, but the paper does not discuss this trade-off. The placeholder normalization replaces identifiers with tokens like FUNC, VAR, and TYPE, which changes the nature of the task by removing useful lexical hints, calling conventions, and library traces. The paper presents the setup as a direct measurement of reverse-engineering ability, which is debatable.

The reproducibility statement is weaker than it sounds because crucial parts of the protocol are not fully pinned down in the main paper. The paper says results will be 'similar, but not identical,' but without clearer reporting of seeds, decoding parameters, parsing stability, and fine-tuning selection criteria, reproducibility remains weak, especially in a low-score regime where a shift from 0.02 to 0.05 can change model rankings.

Please formally define the name-recovery metric, explicitly providing a mathematical definition of how CodeWordNet similarity is converted into precision, recall, and F1 when there are multiple identifiers per sample.

Please report a manual audit on a representative subset (e.g., 200 samples per model) comparing automated extraction against human parsing to validate the accuracy of the auxiliary LLM-based extraction step, including the extraction error rate and how often it changes correctness labels or F1.

Please define the exact target set for function name recovery in decompiled code (whether it is only the enclosing function name, the enclosing function plus all callees, or only callees) and the matching procedure, as the wording in Page 2 and Page 5 is not sufficiently precise.

Please provide the missing fine-tuning details in the main paper, including at minimum: LoRA rank, alpha, target modules, learning rate, batch size, number of epochs or total steps, sequence length, optimizer, decoding settings, and model selection criterion.

Can the authors include task-specific baselines from prior reverse-engineering work? Even if direct reproduction for all methods is too costly, a comparison against at least one specialized baseline for variable names and one for type inference would greatly improve the scientific value of the paper.

Please analyze the strong optimization-level and architecture effects instead of relegating them to appendices or side tables. For example, explain why some models show large gains at O0 but not O2/O3, and why ARM variable-name recovery appears more favorable than x86-64.

How much do the conclusions depend on decoding choices and prompt template choices? A sensitivity study over temperature, max tokens, and prompt template variants could materially affect the conclusion that models are uniformly poor.

For the firmware experiment, please provide dataset details and sample size, including how many firmware images/functions were used, from what sources, under what architectures, and how gold names/types were obtained.

The central theoretical claim (Theorem 3.2) is closer to an intuition sketch than a rigorous result. The update is stated as $\theta^{t+1} = \theta^t + \nabla L_{s_1}(\theta^t)$, while Equation (2) includes a factor $\eta$; the theorem statement and the bound are therefore inconsistent unless one silently absorbs the learning rate into the update.

The term $\lambda_{\max}(J_{\theta^t}(x_1))$ is not well defined if $J_\theta = \partial h(x)/\partial \theta$ is a general Jacobian, since this matrix is not necessarily square; presumably the authors mean an operator norm or largest singular value, but that is not what is written.
The proof in Appendix C introduces an $O(\epsilon)$ term without a precise definition and silently drops the Jacobian-difference term with only a hand-wavy "$O(\epsilon)$" argument.

The core selector $\tau(x,y,t)$ and the quantity $I_{\mathrm{con}}$ are underspecified in the main paper, which makes the algorithm hard to pin down scientifically. In Definition 3.3, $I_{\mathrm{con}}(x,y,\theta)$ is defined as either a loss difference or, alternatively, "we can calculate class-wise accuracy change." Then in Equation (5), $\tau(x,y,t)$ depends on $I_{\mathrm{con}}(x,y,\theta_{t_1})$ and threshold $\beta$, but the actual operational choice is unclear from the main text.

The paper relies on prior knowledge about the target structure that weakens the claimed generality, especially in target mismatch. On Page 3, the authors explicitly assume "that the number of classes in $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{un}}$ belonging to the target concept is known in target mismatch forgetting." This is a strong assumption. In practice, when the whole point is that the target concept does not align with the training taxonomy, knowing in advance how many extra classes belong to the concept is already substantial semantic supervision.

The evaluation protocol mixes task-specific label spaces and then compresses everything into one averaged "Gap," which is convenient but scientifically muddy. In model mismatch, UA/RA/TA are evaluated using superclass labels, while in all-matched and target mismatch they are evaluated using class labels. Then the paper reports a single averaged gap to retraining, giving equal weight to UA, RA, TA, and MIA. This means the same "Gap" is aggregating metrics with different semantics across settings.

There are substantial notation inconsistencies and table/presentation errors in the main paper, enough to slow down careful reading. On Page 3, the dataset notation flips between $\mathcal{D}_l$, $\mathcal{D}_t$, $\mathcal{D}_f$, $\mathcal{D}_r$, $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{un}}$, and related sets, sometimes with apparent OCR or typesetting corruption in Table 1. Equation (1) has a typo in the underbrace label and a confusing statement of the retraining objective. Remark 3.3 is used twice for different remarks. In Table 3, the TARF rows are visibly misaligned.

The claim that the method "approaches retraining" is not really established beyond heuristic optimization behavior. The language around Equations (3) and (4) and the discussion of Phase III suggests that TARF progressively approximates the retraining objective. But this is not shown in any formal sense, nor is there a direct trajectory analysis of distance to retrained parameters or outputs.

The computational story is mixed, and the efficiency claims are weaker than the tables first suggest. In Table 3, TARF is often much slower than GA or other cheap baselines, sometimes by an order of magnitude, though still faster than full retraining. The issue is that the paper sometimes frames TARF as generally efficient, while its target-identification step requires scanning remaining data and computing ranking signals.

Some baselines are strong, but the comparison protocol still leaves room for concern about whether TARF is benefiting from more task-specific adaptation than the baselines receive. TARF is explicitly tailored to the new mismatch settings while most baselines are used more or less off-the-shelf. That is not inherently unfair, but it does mean the headline is partly "a method designed for this problem beats methods designed for a different assumption."

The paper’s use of attack terminology and privacy metrics is sloppy in places. On Page 7 the text defines MIA as Membership Inference Attack, which is standard, but Appendix B.2 calls it "Model Inversion Attack" while describing a confidence-based membership inference predictor. These are not the same thing.

The application sections are interesting but too thin to carry much evidentiary weight in the main-paper argument. Figure 6 and Table 5 are presented as real-world applications, but in the main paper they are under-explained and partly reliant on appendix details. The TOFU table is also difficult to parse as presented, with formatting irregularities and little context on what the numbers mean relative to standard baselines.
The core scoring modification in Equation 2 is heuristic, and the paper does not provide a convincing statistical justification for why SHAP magnitudes should divide the BIC complexity term.

The claimed “consistency remark” is overstated and not established by the paper, as preserving the O(log N) growth is not enough to guarantee BIC-style consistency when a graph-dependent factor is introduced.

The directional signal extracted from SHAP is not clearly justified as causal or even orientation-specific evidence, as predictive asymmetry can be influenced by variable cardinalities, class imbalance, redundant predictors, and model inductive bias.

The use of absolute SHAP values in Equation 3 may discard information that is important for the claimed directional interpretation, and the paper never discusses why magnitude alone is the right statistic rather than a signed, normalized, variance-aware, or pairwise contrastive quantity.

The evaluation protocol disadvantages at least some baselines, especially PC, and likely inflates the reported directed-edge gains by randomly orienting undirected edges from PDAGs before computing directed-edge metrics.
The baseline set is limited for the paper’s stated claim, and the positioning against existing discrete BN structure learning methods is incomplete, particularly the exclusion of MMHC.
The reported gains are modest relative to the computational overhead, and the paper does not convincingly analyze the cost-benefit trade-off.

Several important experimental details are underspecified or internally inconsistent, such as the use of an RMSE objective for a classification task in Optuna tuning, the unclear default value of the confidence threshold, and the incomplete definition in Algorithm 1 when |S_i|=0.

The results presentation is selective, and some tables make it difficult to assess whether the method is consistently better in a statistically meaningful sense, as Table 2 only reports F1 deltas and Table 4 aggregates across 700 runs.

Figure-based evidence only partially supports the main story and also exposes instability that the paper does not discuss enough, such as precision varying substantially with wide uncertainty in Figure 2(e) and (f).

The exposition is decent at the pipeline level, but some core causal distinctions are blurred, sliding into language suggesting that local SHAP asymmetries provide “directional evidence” in a stronger sense than justified.
The claimed evaluation framework is much less general than the paper’s framing suggests, because it depends heavily on simulator-specific privileged access and handcrafted tools.
The experimental comparison may overstate the advantage because the baselines are relatively weak and not matched to the tool-access setting.
The benchmark is small, and the paper does not adequately quantify annotation reliability.
The paper’s formalization is too thin for a method paper built around multi-stage planning and validation.

Some evidence in the paper directly undermines the authors’ own qualitative claims, specifically Figure 8 labeling a judgment as 'Valid' while the explanation states the constraint cannot be satisfied.

The ablation study is weaker than the prose claims, and one of its own numbers cuts against the 'all tools are indispensable' narrative, as removing multimodal reasoning only drops holistic F1 by -0.04%.
The generation benchmark in Table 3 is partially confounded by hybridization with Holodeck, which blurs what is actually being compared.
The presentation is serviceable but noticeably rough, with multiple inconsistencies and errors that obstruct careful reading.
The paper does not sufficiently separate evaluation reliability from benchmark-specific engineering.

The main claim about supporting 'a broad range of relationships expressed in natural language' is only partially substantiated because the experiments mainly report aggregate metrics and broad constraint categories, not breakdowns by challenging relation subtype.

The central importance-ratio approximation is only weakly justified, and the math in the main paper overstates what is actually established. The main text states the approximation error is O(epsilon), but the appendix derives a first-order statement for the log likelihood under additional assumptions, which are not the same object. The appendix even says 'we thus correct the conclusion from the main text', meaning the main-paper statement is not cleanly aligned with the actual derivation.

The argument for the approximation depends on assumptions such as ||delta_vt|| <= epsilon and a Lipschitz constant L_delta = O(epsilon), which are precisely the nontrivial quantities one would need to justify from the optimization dynamics, meaning the theory is largely conditional on the approximation already being benign.

There are mathematical and notation inconsistencies around the PPO objective and state distribution. In Equation (2), the outer expectation is written as E_{p_pi(s)}, but the text immediately below refers to p_{hat_pi}(s) as the policy's state distribution, which is inconsistent with standard PPO notation where one optimizes using states sampled from the old/reference policy.

The Brownian regularizer's connection to actual entropy regularization is much looser than the prose suggests. The actual regularizer does not regularize the policy entropy, nor does it derive from an explicit lower bound on entropy growth, making it closer to a heuristic velocity-field penalty than a principled entropy objective.

The empirical comparisons are incomplete in places where they matter most. On IsaacLab, the paper compares only against PPO and explicitly omits FPO/DPPO due to engineering difficulty, which weakens the paper's positioning because the main novelty is precisely in the context of expressive generative policies.

Some of the claimed benchmark conclusions are stronger than what the presented numbers support. The text around Table 1 says PolicyFlow 'consistently matches or surpasses PPO across all tasks,' but PolicyFlow is numerically lower on Open-Drawer, Quadcopter, H1, and Go2, and has a statistically significant loss on H1.

The MuJoCo Playground discussion says PolicyFlow achieves performance comparable to or exceeding FPO in most environments and outperforms DPPO, yet Figure 3 is only a set of learning curves without a summarized terminal-performance table or statistical comparison, making that claim difficult to verify rigorously.

Fairness of experimental budgets is not fully convincing, especially on MultiGoal. FPO is given 4096 parallel environments, 32 minibatches, 16 epochs, and 1.2x10^8 total environment steps, while PolicyFlow is given 1024 environments and 5 epochs, which are not obviously matched compute or sample budgets.

The strongest qualitative figure is persuasive, but it also exposes how narrow the evidence for multimodality really is. The figures mainly establish that the regularizer helps on specially structured multimodal navigation problems, but do not show that multimodal action distributions are actually important in the higher-dimensional locomotion/manipulation tasks where most of the benchmark weight lies.

Equation-level implementation details that affect reproducibility are underspecified in the main paper. It is unclear whether sigma^2 is state-independent or state-dependent, how it is parameterized and constrained positive, whether the same sampled t_k is reused across epochs, and whether the expectation in Eq. (10) is estimated with one sample or multiple samples per transition.

The exposition is rough in several places, including typos and citation issues. Examples include 'PolicyFlow demonstrates is widely favored' in the abstract, 'velocity filed variations' below Equation (13), 'we purpose a practical entropy regularizer' above Equation (15), and several inconsistent symbols such as w_h vs. w_b in Tables 10 and 15.

The paper's central 'oracle' (GPT-4o) is not really an oracle, and too much of the argument rests on it without adequately quantifying its uncertainty or discussing its trust assumptions in the main text.
The RL evidence is too narrow to support broader claims, as it is overwhelmingly based on a single policy model (Qwen2.5-7B Base) and one main dataset (DeepscaleR).

The comparison between verifier classes is not fully controlled in the static evaluation, because Table 1 evaluates model-based verifiers only on the subset that the rule-based verifier rejected, rather than on the full distribution.

The trained-verifier analysis is underpowered and confounded because the negative result hinges on one custom model (R1-Distill-Verifier-1.5B) trained on a small, narrow dataset, making it impossible to disentangle whether the vulnerability is due to fine-tuning per se, the specific recipe, or the dataset.

Key metrics and evaluation choices are not fully justified and reporting is selective, such as reporting 'best result from each run' and mixing heterogeneous evaluation regimes (Avg@32 vs single-sample) in the average score without discussing variance.

There is an important methodological asymmetry between generative and discriminative verifiers in the robustness probe, as the evaluation pipeline gives generative models a prompt-following surface that discriminative models do not expose, conflating verifier architecture with interface attack surface.

The paper claims trends more strongly than the evidence supports, such as asserting that recall worsens as models get stronger because complex queries are misjudged, when other factors like formatting or output length could explain the trend.

The paper lacks a deeper mathematical or algorithmic analysis of why verifier errors interact with GRPO the way they do, and the exact reward mapping and hybrid composition rule are underspecified in the main text.

The presentation has inconsistencies and sloppiness, such as an internally contradictory statement in Section 5.2 referring to R1-Distill-Verifier-1.5B as the 'untrained verifier' when it is the trained one, and awkward phrasing.

The literature positioning is not fully convincing for a paper making a benchmark-style robustness claim, as the framing is narrow and math-centric rather than systematically discussing verifier evaluation as a broader research problem.

The theoretical justification is much weaker than the paper suggests, and Theorem 1 does not really establish the main claim. The theorem only gives an upper bound on CosSim(M_Q, q*) under assumptions involving a single key, which does not imply that such a query interacts strongly with many keys, nor does it show optimality of the proposed ranking score for approximating attention over a chunk of queries.

Several mathematical formulations are underspecified or imprecise, making it harder to assess the method rigorously. For example, Equation (4) is not a well-defined optimization problem as written because the codomain of f, the admissible dependence of K_hat/V_hat on f, the norm being used, and whether causality inside the chunk is preserved are not specified.

In Algorithm 1, line 2 defines M_Q but the tensor axes are not defined before the algorithm. Line 8 reshapes with a particular layout corresponding to GQA, which implicitly assumes divisibility and a particular layout that should be stated explicitly in the main paper.

In Section 3.3, the statement that pre-aggregation 'achieves the same average' after normalization relies on linearity, but the exact equality is only true for the particular aggregation order used in the algorithm. The paper should clearly show the identity being used, otherwise it reads like hand-waving around a nontrivial implementation choice.

The exposition sometimes overstates what the figures demonstrate. Figure 2(b) is a 2D PCA projection from one layer/head of one model, and proximity in the projected plane is not reliable evidence of actual angular alignment in the original space.

Figure 2(c) shows a correlation between S_q and log(max_k A) with reported correlation 0.737, but that is a correlation for a single analyzed head and does not establish robustness across layers, models, or prompt types. The paper uses these visuals to motivate a fairly general claim about query informativeness, yet the evidence shown in the main paper is narrow and anecdotal.

The comparison space is incomplete for the specific design choice of representative-query selection. The paper does not compare against simpler or alternative representative-query selection strategies that are much closer to its own proposal, such as selecting high-norm queries, selecting queries with largest variance contribution, stratified sampling across positions, or cluster-based representatives.

The empirical evaluation is weaker on realistic end-to-end downstream settings than the claims imply. In Table 3, the main paper only reports normalized averages rather than raw task-level scores, variance, or per-task behavior. Since some entries exceed 1.0, the average can hide both improvements and regressions on specific tasks.

Some of the efficiency claims are not as cleanly supported as the paper suggests, because method overhead is not fully unpacked in the main text. The main paper does not decompose runtime into selection overhead versus reduced attention cost, which matters because on shorter contexts or on hardware with different memory/computation balance, the crossover point may move substantially.

The headline claim in the abstract mixes attention speedup and TTFT speedup. Since TTFT includes non-attention costs, a more careful decomposition in the main paper would help establish how much of the system-level gain is attributable to attention sparsification rather than incidental pipeline effects.

There are several clarity and consistency issues that are distracting and occasionally confusing, such as repeated use of 'prefetch' where the paper clearly means 'prefill' (e.g., in Figure 1 caption and Section 3), inconsistencies in capitalization and naming (QuoKA/QUOKA/Quoka), and some table/model names appearing malformed in the appendix.

Some baseline names in the main paper are inconsistent with references or table labels, for example 'LESSISMORE' in text versus 'LevelsMere' in Table 1. This makes it unnecessarily hard to parse the results and raises concern about possible transcription issues.

The paper argues hardware agnosticism, but the evidence is still narrower than that claim sounds. The runtime evidence in Figure 5 covers A100, one Xeon CPU, and an RTX 2080, which is useful but not enough to justify broad claims across accelerators. The method also depends heavily on efficient dense GEMM/topk/gather implementations, and those primitives can behave very differently on mobile NPUs, DSPs, or edge-class accelerators, which are highlighted in the introduction.

The core claim about 'task ID leakage' is plausible, but the paper does not establish it with the level of rigor needed for such a strong indictment of prior evaluation practice. The empirical evidence in Table 1 is not really an apples-to-apples test of the claimed leakage mechanism... it does not explicitly report the task-ID prediction accuracy for each method... It also does not compare against a controlled variant where local testing is modified to remove graph-identity cues while keeping other factors fixed.

The evaluation protocol may overcorrect by removing inter-task edges and rebalancing classes, which weakens the claim of being 'more realistic'. Removing them may make the benchmark cleaner, but it also changes the problem and potentially suppresses the exact structural transfer that graph methods are supposed to exploit.

The proposed method is effective, but the novelty is fairly modest and the paper does not convincingly separate method contribution from benchmark/protocol contribution. SimGCL is essentially a combination of graph-text prompting, first-session LoRA tuning, and prototype-based classification. Each ingredient is standard on its own...

The mathematical specification of the prototype classifier is incomplete/inconsistent. In Equation (1)... it is unclear whether, when an old class reappears, the prototype is recomputed from all historical labeled samples, updated via a running average, or stored once and never revisited.

Equation (2) is written as a scaled cosine similarity, not a probability, despite the surrounding sentence saying 'its probability of belonging to class j is formulated as follows'. If the authors intend logits, say logits. If they intend probabilities, a normalization... is needed.

There are several notation and formulation problems that reduce confidence in the technical precision. In the FSNCIL formulation on Page 3, the paper writes G_{s_i} intersect G_{s_i} = C_{s_i} intersect C_{s_j} = emptyset for all i != j, which is clearly malformed... In Section 3.1, the notation for the global class set is also awkward...

The empirical comparison is broad but not always fair or sufficiently transparent. The methods operate with different backbones and capacities... some conclusions about 'LLMs alleviate catastrophic forgetting' blur together the benefits of pretraining, model scale, and the actual continual-learning strategy. A cleaner comparison would isolate whether the gain comes from the continual-learning design rather than simply replacing a small GNN with a much larger pretrained backbone.

Some of the strongest claims in the discussion are too causal relative to the evidence provided. For example, on Pages 6-8, the paper attributes GLM underperformance to 'inter-modal misalignment', 'overfitting tendencies', or sparse structural information. These are plausible hypotheses, but the presented results are largely observational... The paper often jumps from correlation to explanation.

The headline gains should be contextualized more carefully. The abstract and introduction emphasize improvements of around 20%. In the main tables, SimGCL is indeed substantially stronger than GNN baselines, but a more relevant comparison is often against SimpleCIL... The claim is directionally true, but the framing is a bit selective.

The presentation in the main paper is uneven, with too many grammatical and naming inconsistencies for a benchmark paper. Examples include 'consists an ordered sequence' on Page 2, 'overperform' on Page 7, inconsistent metric notation between A, A_N, A_hat, and naming mismatches such as GCNLLMEmb / GCN_Emb / GCNsub in different places.

The figure-based evidence is mixed: useful for intuition, weak for decisive support. Figure 3 on Page 8 is used to support scaling claims, but it only shows Arxiv and only compares backbone size for SimpleCIL and SimGCL. That is suggestive, not systematic. Likewise, the qualitative embedding visualization in Figure 4... lacks quantitative cluster metrics in the main paper...
The dataset construction is adaptive and partially target-driven, which raises concerns about selection bias and makes some aggregate statistics harder to interpret cleanly.

The annotation reliability analysis is too optimistic, and the mathematical argument used to infer per-judge error rate is overly simplistic because it assumes independent judges with identical symmetric error rates and no ambiguity effects.
The human-level judge claim is slightly oversold relative to the evidence in the main paper because the human baseline is not measured on the same test subset as the model judges.

The comparison between natural-language and formal proof generation is informative but not fully apples-to-apples, as it compares general-purpose LLMs generating informal proofs to a specialized formal prover and excludes the strongest cited formal result.

Some experimental claims rely on significance language without an adequate statistical treatment in the main paper, such as stating relative performance differences are significant without an actual paired test.
The best-of-n section is somewhat limited in scope because it studies only one generator model and one main judge family, making it difficult to know how general the observed ranking advantage is.
The contamination discussion is still not fully convincing for the strongest comparative claims because the argument remains indirect and does not actually estimate contamination.
The corpus is heavily concentrated on competition mathematics, which narrows the external validity of several claims about mathematical proof generation.

Some presentation details undermine confidence, especially formatting artifacts and malformed LaTeX delimiters in the prompts sections, and content slips in the appendix tables like labeling IMO as an International competition for university students.

The paper could do more to situate itself against finer-grained proof evaluation and grading setups, and provide a clearer discussion of how binary proof correctness compares to partial-credit or step-level proof grading setups.

The paper's strongest theoretical statement (Theorem 4.1) relies heavily on a monotonicity assumption that is only justified informally in the main text, making the main-paper claim read stronger than what is established.

The paper does not quantify in the main text how often the monotonicity assumption fails across prompts and targets, nor how attack performance degrades when it is loose, which matters for the non-intervention attack story.

The mathematical exposition around the diffusion likelihood is underspecified and occasionally sloppy, such as writing nested integrals over discrete token sequences in Equation (1) instead of sums, without explaining if measure-theoretic shorthand is intended.

Equation (5) presents standard alignment as an informal interpretation rather than the actual training objective used in practice, and the method section slides too freely between intuitive surrogates and real optimization targets.

The pseudocode and training description have inconsistencies that make reproduction harder, such as Algorithm 1 using $r^{(i)}_{t_{\min}}$ when the text says $t_{\mathrm{inter}}$, and line 6 having malformed notation.

Algorithm 2 computes $t_{\mathrm{inter}}$ using batch size $B$ in the denominator, which appears inconsistent with the earlier linear schedule definition on Page 6 where the denominator is total steps $S$, looking like a real typo that changes the curriculum schedule.

The main paper defines $\mathcal D_h$ as harmful query-response pairs, but Appendix D.4.2 says the full BeaverTails dataset including harmless pairs is used, creating an inconsistency that should be resolved.

The architectural breadth of the empirical evaluation is limited because all three evaluated systems are very similar masked diffusion language models, and one (MMaDA) starts from a dramatically different, weak safety baseline (79.7% No Attack ASR), which limits how strongly the paper can claim a general MDLM phenomenon.

The paper does not discuss how sensitive the vulnerability numbers are to the exact style, verbosity, or lexical choice of the harmful targets used for the anchoring attack, which could materially affect ASR since the mechanism relies on specific intermediate tokens.

The utility evaluation shows nontrivial drops on some tasks (e.g., HumanEval dropping from 22.0 to 17.1, and PIQA dropping from 74.4 to 71.6 for LLaDA), which the paper describes too casually as 'no substantial degradation' rather than providing a more careful discussion of task-specific regressions.

There are multiple typographical and naming issues in the main paper tables and text, such as 'SPT' where the baseline appears to be SFT, model names like 'ReNeLMA' where the paper earlier discusses MMaDA, and formatting corruption near the baseline description.

The core evaluation metrics are not yet well aligned with the paper’s stated scientific goal, and in places they are actively misleading. The reported headline outcome in Table 1 is dominated by a very high “Win Rate,” often between 0.89 and 1.00, while the corresponding submitter and reviewer CI pass rates are much lower, typically around 0.54 to 0.71. A metric that saturates near 1.0 for almost every matchup weakens the benchmark’s discriminative power.

The battle protocol remains underspecified in several places, which makes it difficult to understand exactly what is measured. There are multiple descriptions of the protocol in Sections 3.2, 3.3, 4.1, and Algorithm 1, and they do not fully line up. For example, the main text says the reviewer receives +1 if their test fails the submitter’s patch and -1 if it fails the golden patch, while the algorithm says “if Test fails to expose meaningful flaw then Test Agent loses 1 point,” but “meaningful flaw” is not formally defined.

The mathematical formalization is too thin for a paper whose contribution is primarily an evaluation protocol. The phrase “agrees with the golden fix” is not mathematically defined. Does this mean exact diff equality, semantic equivalence as judged by an LLM, equal tests passed, or something else?

The mathematical formalization is too thin for a paper whose contribution is primarily an evaluation protocol. There is no formal joint objective over rounds for the reviewer, whose scoring rule is partly binary, partly CI-based, and partly dependent on the golden patch.

The reviewer is said on Page 6-7 to receive “contextual hints including which parts of the code were most changed by the patch.” This is a powerful asymmetry that effectively leaks patch-localization information. Yet the paper does not formalize this information channel, nor quantify how much it contributes.

The empirical comparison space is narrower than the claims suggest, especially regarding baselines against non-adversarial evaluation. The paper repeatedly argues that static benchmarks miss important behavior, but it never directly demonstrates that SwingArena changes model ranking or reveals errors that a standard non-adversarial repo-level setup would miss in a controlled comparison. A very natural baseline would be the same tasks with the same retrieval pipeline and same patch generation budget, but without reviewer-generated tests or without multi-round interaction.

The RACG study is useful but still methodologically limited, making it hard to isolate what component actually helps. Section 3.3 presents RACG as a combination of BM25 file retrieval, syntax-aware chunking, CodeBERT reranking, and token packing, yet Table 3 only compares “w/ RACG” vs “w/o RACG” and a few retrieval-only variants such as BM25 and Top-k related retrievals. This leaves several unanswered questions: Is the gain coming from chunk granularity, dense reranking, packing policy, or simply from retrieving more relevant files?

The file hit rate results in Table 5/Table 6 reveal some odd behavior, for example BM25 Top-20 hit rate being lower than Top-10, and chunk-based methods also slightly decreasing from Top-10 to Top-20. That can happen depending on metric definition, but then the definition should be clarified because “Top-20” should not intuitively underperform “Top-10” if it means inclusion within a larger set. This suggests either a reporting issue or a nonstandard measurement setup.

Some of the strongest claims are more interpretive than supported. For instance, the text around Table 1 claims “GPT-4o's aggressive patching advantage” and that DeepSeek and Gemini “prioritize correctness and CI stability.” But the evidence for psychological or strategic model tendencies is fairly thin. The table shows differences in SPR, RPR, and win rate, but these metrics conflate many factors, including reviewer quality, retrieval adequacy, prompt fit, and CI policy strictness.

The dataset curation process raises concerns about selection bias and benchmark representativeness. On Page 4, the authors mine repositories by popularity, filter by CI pass success, use an LLM judge for clarity and difficulty, and then apply expert filtering. This may produce a cleaner benchmark, but it also risks selecting issues that are unusually well-specified, tractable, and aligned with the authors’ preferred evaluation style. The main text does not sufficiently characterize how much the filtering changes the distribution of issue types, repository sizes, patch complexity, or CI strictness.

Presentation is decent overall, but there are several inconsistencies and signs of rushed assembly that reduce confidence. The paper has repeated “Battle Protocol” descriptions in Sections 3.2 and 3.3, and some appendix references are inconsistent, for example “Table 6” is discussed on Page 9 while the actual table later appears duplicated as Table 5 and Table 6 with identical contents.

There are also some obvious wording issues, such as “morbidity” being used where “complexity” seems intended on Page 15, and the open-source results in Table 4 appear mislabeled in the self-play rows, for example “Qwen2.5-7B vs Qwen2.5-7B” has reviewer listed as Seed-8B.

The Best@k analysis is underdeveloped relative to the claimed importance of test-time scaling. Figure 3 plots Best@k win rate, but it only appears to use Qwen2.5-Coder-7B self-play at temperature 0.25. This is too narrow to support broader conclusions about scaling behavior in the arena.

The role of the golden patch is potentially problematic and insufficiently discussed. The paper relies on the golden human patch for validation references and for rejecting reviewer tests that fail on the golden patch. This is pragmatic, but real GitHub issues often admit multiple acceptable fixes. If “agreement with the golden fix” is interpreted too strictly, the benchmark may penalize valid alternative repairs.

The paper's novelty claim is weaker than the writing suggests, because the core idea is largely iterative region refinement with a small set of hand-designed tools, combining an existing MLLM backbone, standard image subregion operations, and policy optimization.

The method is under-positioned against relevant alternatives that are very close in spirit, especially training-free or lightly trained iterative zoom/refinement baselines, making it hard to know whether the gains come from the proposed RL-trained tool policy rather than from iterative zooming itself.

The empirical story is uneven across benchmarks, and the paper somewhat overstates generality, as the behavior appears highly backbone-dependent and absolute performance remains poor for the non-UI backbone on UI-Vision.

The evaluation on UI-Vision and OSWorld-G is not strong enough to substantiate the paper's broader significance claims, as the cross-benchmark evidence is more 'sometimes helpful' than 'consistently strong.'

Several parts of the mathematical formulation are underspecified or not fully convincing, especially around the RL objective and stability claims, such as whether the expectation is optimized with the usual sign convention, why the geometric mean token ratio is appropriate for long multi-turn tool trajectories, and what precisely qualifies a sample as 'result-correct' for the auxiliary term.

The reward design has hidden assumptions and possible failure modes that are not discussed, such as intermediate tool calls getting positive signals through IoU even with poor overlap, and the sensitivity to the Crop/Extract reward ratio suggesting the behavior is fragile to reward shaping.

The tool design itself is somewhat ad hoc, and the paper does not justify why these three tools are the right abstraction, such as why quarter crops rather than learned scales, why a fixed 10-pixel stride for color search, and why the find_color reward is tied to a 200x200 window while Table 1 describes a centered w/s x w/s crop.

The data construction and filtering pipeline raises concerns about evaluation bias and reproducibility, as using a powerful external MLLM as a quality controller injects another model's preferences into the training set, and the aggressive filtering may skew the retained examples toward easy, text-heavy, or model-legible interfaces.

The exposition has multiple clarity and notation issues that reduce confidence in technical precision, such as inconsistencies in Algorithm 1, awkwardly formatted bucketing notation, and grammatically rough mixes of prose and formulas in Table 2.

The figures reveal limitations that the paper does not fully confront, such as Figure 3 (left) suggesting performance hinges more on preventing syntax collapse than genuinely better policy learning, Figure 4 (left) making the reward-design contribution look narrower, and Figure 5 missing controls for compute-matched baselines.

The paper's 'sample efficiency' claim is directionally interesting but not fully apples-to-apples, as the compared methods differ not just in sample count, but also in data source, pretraining, synthetic generation pipeline, backbone initialization, and task formulation.

The paper could do a better job separating tool-use capability from underlying backbone strength, as the strongest model is initialized from UI-TARS-1.5-7B which is already a strong GUI-specialized base, suggesting GUI-Spotlight may function primarily as a refinement layer rather than a generally powerful grounding framework.

The paper’s strongest results are derived for a highly idealized similarity family, but the title and several claims are phrased in a much broader, almost law-like way than the evidence really supports. The exact “universal Pareto front” claim is only exact under restrictive assumptions, especially homogeneous spaces or the reduction to the scalar quantity b(ε).

The decision rule in Equations (1) and (2) uses Luce-style normalization over similarities, which is a specific behavioral model, not an inevitable consequence of the representation. The paper does not really justify why this is the correct or even preferred decoder for all the systems discussed later, especially CNNs, LLMs, and VLMs.

There are some issues of mathematical clarity and notation that should be fixed. The most obvious one is in Definition 1 on Page 4, where the text defines the constant similarity function with resolution ε but writes using r instead of ε. Similarly, the paper alternates between talking about S and M as the stimulus space after introducing the bijection.

Some derivational steps are plausible but not sufficiently transparent in the main paper, which weakens confidence in the claimed generality. For instance, Theorem 3 gives compact expressions, but the main text does not communicate the combinatorial intuition particularly well, and the expectation over p∼ν is then set aside by focusing on the homogeneous case. The distinction between “general theorem” and “practically interpreted homogeneous case” should be much sharper.

The CNN result in Figure 5a shows a tradeoff as α and ε vary, but a tradeoff induced by training with a weighted objective is not by itself evidence of a fundamental representational law. Multi-objective optimization usually produces tradeoffs. What would matter is stronger evidence that the observed frontier matches the theoretical structure in a nontrivial way, beyond the generic fact that optimizing one metric can hurt another.

The LLM and VLM experiments in Section 5 are too indirect relative to the theoretical setup. The year-similarity experiments are prompt-based behavioral tests on language models. These curves do show degradation away from reference dates, but that could reflect many things, such as inconsistent instruction following, world-knowledge sparsity, tokenization quirks for numerals, or prompt-template artifacts. Likewise, the spatial VLM maps do not isolate “finite semantic resolution” from simpler confounds like visual localization difficulty or answer-format instability.

The scope of comparison to prior work is somewhat thin for such an ambitious positioning. The reader is still left without a very crisp statement of what is genuinely new relative to prior cognitive-science formulations of the generalization-vs-identification tension. The paper would benefit from a more surgical positioning statement, because right now novelty is spread across several partial contributions, which makes it harder to judge the advance.

The paper repeatedly uses language like “universal laws,” “fundamental limits,” and “foundational informational constraints,” especially in the abstract and discussion, but the empirical evidence is not broad enough to support such sweeping wording. The theory is exact for a stylized decoder and stylized similarity classes. The toy model supports the mechanism; the larger-model experiments are consistent with it but far from definitive. This mismatch between evidence and rhetoric matters because it can lead readers to over-interpret what has been established.

The main paper lacks stronger quantitative evaluation of theory-versus-experiment fit in the realistic settings. For the CNN and large-model experiments in Figure 5, the paper mostly gives qualitative correspondence, not rigorous fit tests or falsifiable alternatives. If the paper wants to argue that the same law appears across architectures, this is precisely where one would want stronger quantitative backing.

There is also a mild internal inconsistency in the exposition of the toy model loss. The main paper says the model is trained to perform 3-item similarity tests, but the theory emphasized in the main figures and discussion is mostly the 2-item tradeoff. That makes the comparison in Figure 4b slightly less clean than it initially appears. The paper could do more to explain why plotting the observed trajectory in the same (pS,pI) plane remains the right comparison object across these task variants.

The core novelty is somewhat narrow, and the paper does not position that limitation sharply enough. At a method level, UniMoD is essentially MoD plus task-specific routers plus a heuristic layer-selection scheme based on ARank.

The empirical analysis is interesting but not yet convincing enough as the causal basis for the method design. The jump from 'ARank differs' to 'use per-task routers and these specific MoD placements' is heuristic rather than tightly validated.

The mathematical presentation around the objectives and routers is sloppy in ways that make the method harder to trust. There are multiple notation issues in Equations (2)-(4) and a conflict between thresholding and top-K routing.

ARank is used as a central design signal, but its definition and interpretation are not sufficiently justified. The connection between matrix rank and token-level pruneability is asserted rather than validated.

The pruning-ratio estimation is very heuristic and not well specified enough for reproducibility. It leaves several missing details: what exact normalization formula is used, how ratios are clipped, whether task-specific ratios are smoothed across layers, etc.

The baselines are too weak for the central empirical claim. The strongest baseline is relegated to an ablation rather than promoted to the main table, lacking a careful head-to-head against a strong generic MoD adaptation with tuned capacities and tuned layer placement.
The gains on Show-o are modest and the metric tradeoff is less clean than the prose suggests. Some understanding metrics drop, and the current wording oversells the consistency of the improvement.
The Emu3 evaluation is hard to interpret because the training setup differs materially from the original model, and the paper relies on this model for one of its strongest efficiency claims.

The analysis of layer importance is too narrow to support the design rule used later. Observation 2 is based on skipping odd-numbered layers in Show-o and inspecting GQA performance in Table 1, which is only one task and one benchmark.

The task-competition experiment is intriguing but underdeveloped. It introduces a bespoke router capacity of 0.5 plus a Gumbel-Softmax formulation described only in the appendix, and it is not obvious that this competition setup faithfully reflects the actual UniMoD routing regime.

The clarity and consistency of exposition need work. There are many small but cumulative issues: 'Mixture of Depths' is written as both singular and plural; 'Show-o' and 'Show-o*' are used without immediate clarification; 'UniMod' and 'UniMoD' both appear; some sections use 'sequence redundancy' and 'token redundancy' interchangeably without defining the distinction.

The evidence for scalability beyond two tasks is too weak in the main paper. The actual support is deferred outside the main body, which limits the generality of the contribution for a headline idea of task-awareness.

Some claims about memory and speed are plausible but under-analyzed. Table 4 reports fairly small iteration-time reductions for Show-o despite nontrivial TFLOP reductions, and the paper's discussion is too brief.
The transition from Eq. (2) to Eq. (3) changes the objective rather than deriving it, making the reformulation mathematically shaky.
The EM derivation uses notation that obscures the actual latent variable structure, specifically the auxiliary distribution Q(x_j^{(v_2)}) is independent of i but should be conditional on i.
The claimed convergence story is overstated because the implemented E-step and M-step are approximate, meaning standard EM monotonicity arguments do not automatically apply.
The marginal estimation in Eq. (13)-(14) is under-justified and potentially problematic as a probability model because it is not shown to be normalized across samples.
The reduction to InfoNCE in Proposition 2 / Eq. (19) is mathematically imprecise as written in the main paper because the denominator sums over different things.
The computational cost and scalability are not adequately discussed in the main paper, specifically missing runtime, memory, number of Sinkhorn iterations, and sensitivity to batch size.
The empirical comparison's fairness is not fully transparent because it is not clear whether all baselines use equally strong backbones, augmentations, and optimization settings.
In Table 2, the setting labels are ambiguous with repeated MR blocks but no clearly printed CR values in the left-most column.
The paper's treatment of category-level mismatch is partly definitional rather than fully empirical, stopping short of a direct quantitative evaluation in the main paper.
There are exposition and consistency issues, such as mixing semicolon and conditional notation for probabilities, introducing constant A without explanation, and inconsistent warmup duration.

Core methodological details in Section 4.1 are underspecified, specifically the definition of the active region I_k is not operationally clear enough to reproduce or evaluate because the thresholding rule for 'highly activated residues' is not defined.

There are mathematical and notational issues around Equations (3)-(6), including at least one apparent inconsistency with the underlying model description, specifically Equation (6) defining the D-SCRIPT interaction score as the max contact probability, which contradicts the model description in Section 3.

The evaluation protocol's baseline set is narrow and some key comparisons are missing, such as no simple nearest-neighbor or homology-style retrieval baseline, no baseline using the full embedding without active-region selection, and no ablation showing whether the gain comes from active-region localization versus merely using known-partner embedding similarity.

The main results table (Table 1) is difficult to interpret and contains suspicious regularities, such as MAP@k being numerically identical to Recall@k, and some rows appearing malformed or containing blank cells.

The re-ranking evaluation in Section 5.3 is not strong enough to support the broad conclusions drawn because it only reports the fraction of interactions whose rank was maintained or improved, without showing the magnitude of improvement or whether it occurs near the top of the list, and the paper never reports final end-to-end ranking quality after re-ranking using the same metrics as Table 1.

The paper's main assumption, that novel interactors resemble previously known ones for the same protein, is insufficiently stress-tested because the empirical section does not analyze performance as a function of the number of known partners, target-protein degree, or novelty regime.

Some of the strongest claims are overstated relative to the evidence provided, such as suggesting improvements 'by two orders of magnitude' and a 'step change' in prioritization, while the baseline choice is narrow, the metric table is partially malformed, and the end-to-end re-ranking outcome is not shown in the same standard ranking metrics.

The runtime analysis is only partially fair and only partially actionable because some preprocessing costs are excluded for the semantic methods, which means the comparison is not a full pipeline cost comparison and the practical attractiveness of those methods could be overstated.

Positioning relative to related work is somewhat narrow for a paper making general claims about candidate ranking from modern PPI representations, as the experimental positioning would be stronger with discussion of more recent PPI predictors based on protein language models or graph/hybrid architectures.

The mathematical derivation is inconsistent in several places, specifically regarding the notation around the Gram matrices and cross-covariance matrices in Equations (2) to (8) and Appendix B, which weakens confidence in the closed-form optimization.

The AMP formulation is under-justified and mathematically odd because the norm on the Hadamard product in the objective is unspecified, the passage to the trace expression is not generally equivalent without assumptions, and the masking rule in Equation (10) uses sign yielding {-1,0,1} but is used as a binary selector in {0,1} in Equation (11).

The core claim that selective application to the final FC layer is the right design is only weakly established in the main paper, as the evidence appears only in the appendix on limited models, making it seem like a hand-picked heuristic rather than a robust principle.

The empirical gains over the strongest baseline (ARB-RC) are relatively modest in many entries, and the evaluation does not fully support the strength of the claims, especially since PTB rows are emphasized despite the paper admitting perplexities are too high to be meaningful.

Important experimental details that affect scientific confidence are missing or pushed out of the main paper, such as the number of calibration samples, whether calibration data are fixed, the exact zero-shot evaluation pipeline, hyperparameter tuning, and optimization iterations.

The attention-preservation story is plausible, but the evidence is indirect and architecture-specific, as the paper measures similarity drift in output representations rather than actual attention logits, and the explanation for AMP's varying effect across architectures is only a post hoc hypothesis.

Some figures support the paper's intuition but are not quantitative enough to fully validate the proposed decisions, such as Figure 1 not reporting the magnitude of differences and Figure 2 not directly comparing the proposed remedy against ARB-X.

The paper's novelty relative to existing compensation/refinement-style 1-bit PTQ methods is somewhat narrower than advertised, as it builds directly on ARB-RC parameterization and alternation, making it more of a focused refinement than a substantial methodological departure.

Presentation quality in the method section is uneven and occasionally sloppy, with wording and notation issues such as duplicate arguments in Algorithm 1 and inconsistent layer indexing, which hurts credibility for a paper selling a closed-form optimization procedure.
The benchmark's 'realism' and 'economic value' claims are argued more by assertion and anecdotes than by systematic evidence, and lack actual human baselines or inter-rater difficulty calibration.

The selection process from 229 contributed tasks to 89 final tasks is insufficiently quantified, leaving benchmark composition bias underexplored (e.g., no breakdown of excluded tasks by category or rejection reason).

The comparison between models and agents is not fully apples-to-apples, yet some conclusions (e.g., 'model selection is usually more important than agent scaffold') are phrased too strongly without systematic factorial analysis or variance decomposition.
Terminus 2 is presented as a 'neutral' testbed, but its design choices (e.g., context summarization, Bash-only restriction) are consequential and under-ablated in the main paper.

The error analyses depend heavily on LLM-as-judge pipelines, and the validation is limited for the claims being made (e.g., no confidence intervals on class proportions, no sensitivity analysis to the chosen judge model).

There are numerical and reporting inconsistencies that undermine confidence in the presentation, such as Table 2's caption stating token counts are for 'all 74 tasks' while the benchmark is described as 89 tasks, and Section 3 claiming '16 frontier models' while the list includes more.

The statistical treatment of derived benchmark properties is weak, such as arbitrary thresholds for empirical difficulty categories without sensitivity analysis, and claiming a 'positive correlation' without discussing uncertainty around the empirical difficulty labels.

The benchmark's reproducibility story is mixed, and the paper does not quantify how much run-to-run or platform-to-platform instability affects results, especially given that internet access is allowed.
The absence of actual human or non-LLM operational baselines limits interpretation of the reported scores, especially given the paper's central framing about professional work.

Some results are interesting descriptively but are not connected back to concrete benchmark-design lessons strongly enough (e.g., not analyzing why universally unsolved tasks are unsolved, or whether cost-normalized ranking is stable).
The paper would benefit from sharper positioning relative to adjacent benchmark paradigms, as it is currently vague about what exactly Terminal-Bench should replace versus complement.
Some formal definitions are underspecified given how much they are used, such as how per-model pass rate is estimated for empirical difficulty, and how confidence intervals are constructed.

The central methodological object, the context encoder f(·) in Equation (1), is not sufficiently specified in the main paper. It is unclear if the representation is the final hidden state, a pooled sequence embedding, or the representation at position i, and whether the encoder is frozen.

The mathematical formulation around representation fusion in Equation (2) is weak and somewhat inconsistent. The use of a scalar α to balance two components under concatenation is odd because concatenation does not actually mix the modalities; it only rescales them before stacking, and the paper does not justify this or explain how dimensions/norms are handled.

The adaptive clustering procedure is largely heuristic and the main paper does not provide enough evidence that it is principled or stable. The balancing mechanism is a manually tuned allocation rule rather than a learned or theoretically justified one, and without sensitivity analyses, it is hard to know if improvements are robust or a product of task-specific tuning.

Several parts of the semantic-ID merging procedure are underspecified or mathematically sloppy. The notation for frequencies is inconsistent between the main paper and Appendix E (e.g., mixing C_i and C_{v_i}, inconsistent notation in Equations 4, 7, and 10), and the merge rule depends on whether proximity is measured in token space, fused embedding space, or centroid space.

The training objective and data augmentation are underexplained relative to how central they are to the gains. The exact sequence formatting is not given, and the augmentation strategy may create training examples inconsistent with the original context-conditioned token assignment, which could introduce label ambiguity.

The inference procedure for multi-facet generation is too vague for a method that claims interpretability and personalized probability aggregation. The paper does not formally define how item probabilities are aggregated from beam search paths, which matters because prefix sharing can distort probability mass.

The empirical evaluation is narrower than the claims. All experiments are on three Amazon subsets with relatively short average sequence lengths (8 to 9), which is an awkward setting for a method whose main advantage is leveraging the entire user interaction history.

Key baselines are not fully stress-tested against the paper's own causal story. To support the claim that long-horizon personalized context helps, analyses such as performance broken down by number of semantic IDs per item, user-history length, or item ambiguity level are missing.

The exposition contains multiple notation and presentation issues that make the paper harder to trust, such as fluctuating dataset names, a likely typo referring to S1-Rec instead of S3-Rec, and an obviously inconsistent value in Table 8.

The qualitative evidence is interesting but overstated. Figure 4 relies on a hand-picked game example where the interpretation of semantic IDs comes from external narrative rather than intrinsic disentanglement, and the explainability experiment relies on GPT-4o judgments.

The comparison against static tokenizers may partly entangle tokenizer quality with downstream model/training choices, because Pctx also introduces extra components at training and inference time (augmentation and multi-facet generation).

The paper's conceptual argument about prefix similarity is plausible, but not formally established. The paper never formalizes the degree of this effect or under what decoding model assumptions it holds strongly enough to motivate the entire method.

The paper oversells 'turbulence' and physical fidelity, while the evaluation is still mostly ML-style reconstruction error. The main metrics in Table 1 are MSE, nRMSE, and Max_ERR only, which do not establish that the generated trajectories preserve physically meaningful statistics such as energy spectra, structure functions, enstrophy, invariant preservation, or long-time distributional statistics.

The theoretical analysis in Section 4 is too weak relative to the claims it is used to support. Theorem 4.1 is about the forward corruption process of a simplified diffusion SDE, not about the learned reverse model's actual reconstruction quality. Also, the method proposed is a flow-matching model, yet the theorem mostly critiques diffusion-style corruption. The bridge from 'high frequencies are corrupted earlier' to 'therefore FourierFlow should reconstruct them better' is not established.

The mathematical exposition around the common-mode noise story is not convincing enough, and some claims are under-justified. Section 2.2 argues that adding common-mode noise shifts QK^T by a rank-1 term which 'flattens the softmax distribution and suppresses token discrimination,' but a constant additive term shared across all logits within a row would cancel under softmax, while a general rank-1 perturbation does not necessarily flatten attention uniformly.

Equations (4) to (6) are not fully specified, and the notation is inconsistent enough to hinder reproducibility. There is a conceptual mismatch between the prose and the equation regarding Attn_2 focusing on 'broader background context' while the equation restricts it to local neighbors. Also, the distance metric over patches for the neighborhood N(j) is never specified (spatial-only, spatiotemporal, feature space, etc.).

The Fourier mixing branch has unclear or possibly incorrect wording around mode truncation and high-frequency preservation. The text states, 'Since there is mode truncation to keep high-frequency components,' which is odd because standard Fourier neural operator truncation usually discards high-frequency modes and keeps lower modes, unless the implementation is explicitly reversed.

The surrogate alignment component is underspecified in the main paper. The alignment loss L_Align is never defined mathematically in the main paper, leaving it unclear which layers are aligned, whether features are normalized, what the pointwise loss is, and whether there is a learned projector. This is a major omission because the alignment loss is presented as one of the three main contributions.

There are multiple presentation and consistency problems that reduce trust in the experimental section. For example, the train/test split description is inconsistent (90% training stated below Table 1 vs. 80/10/10 split in Section 5.1). There are also metric naming mismatches (caption says RMSE but columns labeled MSE) and terminology inconsistencies (Fourier-Flow vs. FourierFlow, flow matching vs. CFM vs. L_flow vs. L_CFM).

The empirical comparisons in Table 1 are not as airtight as the paper suggests. The table compares methods with quite different parameter counts (12.4M to 169M), with the proposed model being among the largest (161M).
