The use of LLMs in benchmark construction creates a risk of circularity, and the paper does not quantify annotation quality sufficiently in the main paper (e.g., missing statistics on human validation rate, inter-annotator agreement, correction frequency).

The task taxonomy boundaries are somewhat soft and partly format-driven, entangling reasoning depth, output format, and answer length, which makes it harder to attribute gains to structural reasoning.

Some empirical interpretations overreach what the tables directly support, overstating the advantage of GraphRAG models when the picture is heterogeneous and vanilla RAG remains competitive on some metrics.
The benchmark is still narrow in corpus diversity for a paper making broad practical recommendations, using only two English, text-only corpora.
Presentation quality is hurt by many inconsistencies, typos, and naming errors, some of which interfere with careful reading (e.g., 'LeghtRAG', 'Durren Edge', 'Surfth et al.', 'LapHRAG', 'mucirRAG').

Graph quality metrics are too primitive to support the paper's stronger claims about 'quality graphs', relying on topological summaries rather than semantic correctness, edge precision, or graph faithfulness to source text.
Efficiency analysis is useful but still incomplete as a cost-benefit study, missing latency, indexing cost, and quality-versus-cost frontiers.

The benchmark seems more like an evaluation suite for current systems than a carefully controlled scientific instrument, and the paper does not fully embrace that distinction, speaking in controlled-science language when the setup is a comparative systems study.

The paper’s central conceptual claim, that HES measures “reasoning quality,” is not actually established, and some evidence in the paper points in the opposite direction. If incorrect trajectories can have higher HES on average, then HES is not a clean quality metric in the sense claimed by the title and the method section.

HES is likely heavily confounded with response length, and the paper does not adequately disentangle this. The paper claims the relative threshold makes the metric “robust to variations in length” but provides no derivation or empirical decorrelation analysis.

The mathematical specification of the core metric is sloppy and in places inconsistent. The notation in Equation (1) is ambiguous, the definition of AvgHE in Equation (3) is muddled and self-contradictory, and the set T_high is not rigorously specified for every variant.

The RFT formulation in Section 2.1 is mathematically incorrect or at least badly misstated. It uses argmax to describe selecting a response subset, but argmax returns a maximizing element or set of ties, not a subset of arbitrary size k, which mismatches the actual experiments.

The RL section does not convincingly show that HES is a principled RL signal rather than a batch-curriculum heuristic. The RL experiment is really a selective subsampling strategy within GRPO rollouts, not a replacement reward or a theoretically motivated policy objective.

The experimental setup leaves open serious concerns about evaluation noise and statistical significance. Nearly all conclusions are drawn from single reported averages without variances, confidence intervals, or multiple-run seeds, which matters for small claimed improvements.

The baseline set is not strong enough to justify the breadth of the claims. The paper compares mainly to random, length, heuristic difficulty, average entropy, total entropy, and a few ablations, but lacks engagement with stronger or more targeted data selection strategies.

The claim of “unified” data selection is overstated relative to what is actually demonstrated. The paper presents three rather different uses of the same score (offline subset filtering, candidate ranking among correct traces, and post hoc selector among successful rollouts), which is more accurately “one scalar heuristic applied in several settings,” not a unified formulation.

The paper’s figure-based evidence is suggestive but also reveals some tension with the narrative. Figure 1 shows HES as a discriminator of sample type rather than a direct measure of correctness-aligned quality, and Figure 3 and Figure 4 show peak performance at 20% or 80% retained data but the curves are not universally sharp and gains look modest.

There are several writing and presentation issues that undermine confidence, including duplicated paragraph titles, grammar issues, inconsistent naming, formatting problems in Table 6, and extraneous unrelated content in the appendix.

The computational efficiency claim is under-supported in the main paper. HES requires a full forward pass over every candidate sequence to obtain token entropies, but the cost discussion appears only in the appendix while the main paper makes strong efficiency claims without quantifying the screening overhead.

The domain generalization claims are weaker than advertised. The non-math evidence in Table 3 and Table 4 uses only a few benchmarks, and some results are odd (e.g., HMMT25 behavior), reading more like preliminary transfer checks than a convincing domain-general validation.

The headline equivalence claim is stronger than what the math in the main paper really supports, as the actual result is qualified by multiple strong assumptions and residual terms (span conditions, feasibility, small-edit assumptions).

Several mathematical statements are underspecified or too informal for claims of this breadth, such as the construction of ρ_s in Theorem 4.2 not being written explicitly and the conditions for the converse part not being spelled out carefully.
There are concrete notation and indexing issues that make the technical presentation less trustworthy, such as duplicate equation numbering and alternating cross-references.

The optimization and 'spectral optimality' claim in Theorem 5.3 is not stated with sufficient precision to be verifiable, as 'expected first-order logit change' is not formally defined as a scalar objective and the claimed optimum value introduces a vector-valued term without specifying a norm or scalarization.

The 'generalization under low-rank steering' section is not convincingly connected to the actual intervention studied in the rest of the paper, as an input-dependent activation edit is not obviously representable as a fixed additive rank-k model perturbation.

The no-free-lunch statement in Theorem 6.2 appears too strong as written, because the quantification is unclear regarding what exactly the 'corresponding' parameter perturbation is, risking confusion between subspace projection geometry and a universal amplitude bound.

The empirical evidence is too thin to support the scope of the claims, as the main experiments are very small (GPT-2 Medium in one detoxification setup and a single ResNet-50 class-direction example) to establish robustness across architectures, tasks, or intervention regimes.

The detoxification experiment in Table 1 is not favorable to the proposed method, as IAS is worse than CAA on both reported metrics (toxicity and perplexity) without a careful explanation of why the method is still preferable.

Figure 1 undercuts the paper's own claims, as the reported slope of 1.50 suggests a substantial scale mismatch, meaning 'IAS matches influence at first order' is too generous a caption for what only shows directional agreement.

The cost claims are optimistic and insufficiently substantiated, as the description suppresses the expensive part of influence estimation (applying (H+λI)^-1 at scale) and lacks timing, memory, or approximation-quality analysis.

Some assumptions are strong enough that they deserve either empirical examination or sharper discussion, but the paper mostly treats them as if they were routine (e.g., affine independence assumption, lack of a systematic sweep over steering magnitude α).

The literature positioning is somewhat narrow relative to the paper’s own framing, as the related-work section is quite compressed given the breadth of the claims and does not spend enough effort distinguishing itself from neighboring formulations.
Presentation quality is uneven despite the appealing high-level narrative, as several proofs are only sketched, theorem assumptions drift between sections, and cross-references are messy.
The paper sometimes overstates “precise characterization” while the actual statements are upper bounds with extra logarithmic and structural overheads.

There are several clarity and notation problems in the mathematical exposition, and some are in core definitions rather than harmless typos. A concrete example is Definition 2.4 on Page 4, where the second expression for adaptive smoothness uses ∇^d f(x), which appears to mean the Hessian but is not standard notation and is inconsistent with the surrounding text.

The “Comparison between two smoothness notions” paragraph on Page 5 has a displayed equation that is circular and apparently malformed... As written, the leftmost and rightmost quantities are identical, and the middle ratio mixes H and H in a way that does not match the preceding argument.

Equation (3) on Page 3 is conceptually slippery. The paper “minimizes both sides” of an NSD guarantee over H... But the left-hand side is a post hoc infimum over norms after generating one trajectory {x_t}, whereas the right-hand side is interpreted as saying Adam “automatically identifies the best diagonal norm.” Those are not the same logical statement.

The main algorithms are presented too noisily in the paper body. Algorithm 2 and Algorithm 3 on Page 8 are especially hard to parse because several lines are visibly malformed... For a theory paper whose novelty rests heavily on the exact update rules, this level of typesetting damage is a real presentation weakness.

The acceleration result in Theorem 4.3 rests on a fairly strong and somewhat awkward bounded-iterate assumption, namely max_t ||x_t-x*||_H <= D. The paper acknowledges in Remark 4.4 that D is unknown and then defers the projected fix to Appendix E.2. Since the accelerated guarantee is one of the flagship contributions in the main text, it would help to either present the projected version in the main paper, or at least discuss more explicitly how restrictive the unprojected assumption is.

The stochastic story is interesting, but the noise assumptions are not as operational as the paper makes them sound. Definition 4.1 introduces adaptive gradient variance by minimizing over H in H with Tr(H) <= 1, and then taking a supremum over all t and all x. This is mathematically clean, but from a modeling standpoint it is a strong uniform assumption over the entire domain... it is not clear when σ_H is finite, small, or estimable. This does not invalidate the theorem, but it does limit the usability of the result and should be discussed more candidly.

The paper lacks any empirical or even synthetic quantitative validation. I am not demanding a large-scale deep learning benchmark from a theory submission, but the absence of any small experiment, numerical sanity check, or even toy example is noticeable given the paper’s repeated claims about the “benefit” of adaptive smoothness and adaptive variance.

There are places where the exposition blurs whether the comparison is algorithmic, analytical, or complexity-theoretic. For example, in the introduction and Section 2.1, the paper moves from “Adam without EMA coincides with NSD under the corresponding norm” to “adaptive optimizers and NSD exploit different smoothness notions.” That is a valid high-level message, but the exact sense of “exploit” is not always stable. Is the claim that the methods behave differently, that their known proofs require different assumptions, or that different assumptions are necessary for optimal rates? The paper uses all three flavors at different moments. Tightening this would improve both precision and impact.

Figure 1 only illustrates the diagonal ℓ_∞/ℓ_1 case, even though one of the paper’s main messages is a general theory for arbitrary well-structured preconditioner sets. Given how central the generalization beyond diagonal matrices is, a second visual or example for a noncommutative case would have strengthened the paper. As it stands, the only concrete picture readers get is the easiest commutative setting.

The paper has no quantitative results tables in the main text, which becomes a weakness for assessing empirical support and the practical significance of the theory. Since the central claims are about benefits such as acceleration and dimension-free dependence, the absence of even a small benchmark or ablation table means the reader cannot judge whether these benefits appear in any finite-sample regime or only at the level of asymptotic worst-case theory.

While the appendix is substantial, some claims in the main paper rely on deferred details enough that the main text occasionally feels like a compressed theorem catalog. For a paper with this many moving parts, the authors need to do more in the main text to guide the reader through what is truly new, what follows from prior frameworks, and where the delicate proof steps actually enter.

There is a serious mathematical/sign inconsistency in the key bound on Page 5, and it directly affects the central evaluation quantity. The paper states a lower bound on Pr[False] but the right-hand side behaves like a lower bound on precision (Pr[¬False]), creating a notational and logical inconsistency.

The central assumptions are much stronger and more fragile than the paper acknowledges, especially in the actual HMDA setting. Assumption 1 states independence of origination decisions across borrowers, but within the algorithm's highly specific partitions, origination outcomes are plausibly correlated through local market conditions, underwriting standards, etc.

Assumption 2 is under-motivated and not obviously appropriate for the quantity it is used to bound. The monotonicity in the number of submitted applications is not empirically checked and is not clearly justified in the mortgage-shopping context, as borrowers who submit more applications could be systematically weaker or rejected more often.

The experimental evaluation is too insular, because the paper evaluates only one clustering family and essentially no competing unsupervised evaluation schemes. There is no comparison to other linkage strategies or existing unsupervised record-linkage/entity-resolution evaluation approaches.

The literature positioning is incomplete for a paper whose central claim is about unlabeled evaluation of record linkage. The manuscript contains no dedicated related work section and cites almost no directly comparable prior work on unsupervised linkage evaluation.

The model-selection story is less principled than advertised because the distance functions are largely hand-crafted and weakly justified. The candidate distances include ad hoc constructions with hard-coded constants, and there is little explanation of where these choices come from or whether the results are sensitive to them.

The main empirical application provides no ground-truth validation, only indirect diagnostics, so the headline 92.3% precision remains hard to trust. The paper could evaluate on a subset with external linkage signals, synthetic perturbations, or controlled holdouts, but relies on theoretical bounds and qualitative diagnostics.

Several presentation and notation choices make the technical argument harder to follow than necessary. There is recurrent slippage between clusters, applications, and applicants, and confusing index switching in Equation (3).

The simulation evidence is helpful but not sufficiently stress-tested. The simulation appears designed to be congenial to the method and does not probe failure modes, such as correlated originations, negative association with shopping success, or non-identical legitimate repeat applications.

The claimed recall contribution is weaker than the framing suggests. Because P_tot is unknown, the paper can only rank specifications by a quantity proportional to the lower bound, not compute recall itself, but the abstract and introduction make the contribution sound stronger.

The paper repeatedly leans on appendix-only evidence for claims that matter in the main narrative. For example, the simulation recall value of 92% and the application validation are deferred to the appendix, but the strongest empirical support should not be offloaded there.
The main paper does not cleanly isolate which component is responsible for which gain, and the main paper does not provide a sufficiently systematic decomposition across all settings.

The mathematical formulation of the tokenizer objective is incomplete and somewhat inconsistent with standard RVQ/VQ training, underspecifying the actual training dynamics and creating avoidable ambiguity about whether the loss is applied before or after unpatchifying.

The BAR objective in Equation (3) glosses over a nontrivial train-test mismatch, and the description around Figure 3(c) does not provide enough detail to verify that the stated objective and the implemented mask are actually consistent.
The novelty relative to recent action-tokenization work is somewhat overstated in places, as the actual methodological ingredients are mostly a careful assembly of known ideas.
Some central empirical claims are supported primarily by custom metrics or by appendix-only evidence, and the main paper does not always give enough calibration.
Baseline fairness is not fully transparent, especially where pretraining sources and tokenizer data differ, creating some uncertainty about apples-to-apples comparison.

The practical narrative is a bit selective regarding efficiency gains, as the biggest runtime component is observation encoding, not action decoding, and FASTerVLA and pi_0 have similar runtimes in the whole-body setting.
Presentation quality is mixed, with multiple notational and editorial issues that matter more than they should in a technical paper.
The codebook-usage analysis is suggestive but not yet fully persuasive as a mechanistic explanation, reading more as a correlation than a demonstrated mechanism.
The main paper under-discusses failure modes and robustness limits, with little qualitative analysis of where FASTer still fails or whether BAR introduces characteristic failure patterns.

The theoretical analysis in Section 5 is much weaker than the paper claims, and parts of it appear internally inconsistent. Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 study a stylized surrogate model rather than the proposed method itself, but the paper presents it as establishing the actual behavior of SSA in practice.

There are multiple notation and derivation problems that make the method difficult to verify. Equation (8) is problematic, the local term is underspecified, and dimensional consistency is not obvious. Equation (11) inherits the same issue, and the 'presynaptic input' mixes terms in a way that is more descriptive than formally defined.

Equation (12) abruptly introduces Token_n[t], A, and Gamma without giving a derivation that shows how this is an approximation of Equation (11). By the time we reach Equations (13) and (15), the symbols have drifted again.

The claimed memory and complexity reductions are not cleanly established. The manuscript mixes several different notions of storage complexity (storing QK matrices, KV matrices, membrane states, etc.) and never provides a precise accounting protocol (e.g., peak activation memory vs. persistent state memory).

The causal claim that locality mismatch is the main reason for the performance gap is overstated. Many other factors differ between VSA and SSA, and the paper does not isolate locality as the dominant factor.

The empirical evidence is incomplete for the paper's central claims because the paper does not report variance across runs, confidence intervals, or whether the reported gains are single-run numbers, which is particularly important when margins are small.

The segmentation results in Table 2 are hard to interpret because the table organization is confusing and some comparisons are not apples-to-apples. LRF-SSA appears to add a substantial number of parameters, which sits awkwardly with the earlier claim that it introduces 'almost no additional parameters.'

The relationship between LRF-SSA and LRF-Dyn is not adequately validated as an approximation claim. There is no direct approximation study comparing attention outputs or feature similarity between the two, and similar empirical performance alone does not establish that the dynamics implement attention in the proposed sense.

Some claims around biological inspiration feel more rhetorical than scientifically operationalized. The paper leans heavily on biological terminology without always showing how these constructs materially constrain or justify the architecture, and the actual implementation reads like a custom recurrent filtering module.

There are concrete mathematical inconsistencies in the appendix that reduce confidence in the theorems summarized in the main paper. For example, Equation (3) is labeled as SSA but gives an exponential form, and the notation flips between alpha, a, lra-ssa, and lrf-ssa.

Presentation quality is below the level expected for a method paper with this many equations. There are many grammar and wording issues, and the notation is not stable across sections, which is a serious presentation problem for a paper whose main novelty is a new mathematical reformulation.

The literature positioning around efficient or locality-aware spiking attention is somewhat thin. The related work discussion is quite narrow relative to the claimed contribution, making the method look more isolated than it actually is, which weakens the novelty argument.

The qualitative figures are supportive but also expose gaps in the evaluation protocol. The paper does not quantify sparsity, entropy, or localization improvements across the dataset, and the exact memory metric and measurement setup for Figure 5(b) are not stated.

The empirical scope is too narrow to support the broader claims made in the paper. All results are on highly synthetic, low-dimensional tasks with hand-designed compositional structure... It does not yet show that the approach remains effective when modules are only approximately reusable, when the task grammar is noisy, or when observations are higher-dimensional and ambiguous.

The baseline suite is underdeveloped and somewhat favorable to the proposed method. The main baselines are a vanilla RNN without task identity, an RNN with task identity, and a version of the proposed architecture with flat transitions. These do not meaningfully test whether the gains come from probabilistic inference per se, from modular decomposition, or simply from stronger task-structured inductive bias.
The discussion cites related modular/meta-learning work such as Alet et al. and Hummos et al., but no empirical comparison is provided, not even on the toy domains.

The paper also claims on Page 3 that this is 'fundamentally different' from common meta-learning approaches, yet the only gradient-based comparisons in Figure 3e,f are variants of a task-ID RNN. That is a very weak proxy for the broader class of latent-task-inference or modular meta-learning methods.

The main text on Page 2 defines z_t ~ Cat(W_G g_t) in Equation 2, but does not specify whether W_G g_t are logits or probabilities. A categorical distribution requires normalized probabilities, so some softmax-like transformation is implicit but omitted.

Equation 3 suggests there is a single module hidden state m_t, whereas the architecture actually contains N module RNNs. The appendix on Page 14 says the implementation uses a soft activation vector across modules during training and then 'sum[s] the hidden state across all modules, weighted by the activation vector.' That is materially different from the main-text description of selecting one module and propagating its state. It is therefore unclear whether unselected modules keep persistent hidden states, whether all modules are updated every step during training, or whether there is only one shared recurrent state carried by the active module.

There is a second issue around differentiation through the particle filter. On Page 3, the paper says it optimizes -log L by 'backpropagating the loss through the particle filter' and uses Gumbel-softmax for gradients through Equation 2. But the filter also contains the resampling step in Equation 6, which is discrete and ancestor-dependent. The paper does not explain whether gradients stop at resampling, whether a straight-through estimator is used, or whether only pre-resampling likelihood terms contribute gradients.

In Equation 5 on Page 3, the paper writes l_t^{(k)} = p(y_t | z_t^{(k)}; Lambda) = p(y_t | mu_t^{(k)}; Lambda). Strictly speaking, the likelihood is not a function of z_t alone, but of the particle's predictive latent state, including the relevant hidden states g_t^{(k)}, m_t^{(k)}, which themselves depend on the whole ancestral path. The main-paper notation obscures it.

In Section 2.3 the paper alternates between filtering and smoothing style quantities. For example, it says it plots p(z_t | y_{1:t}) but then overlays red dots labeled as arg max_{z_t} p(z_t | y_{1:T}) in Figure 2d and Figure 4d,e. Those are different posterior objects. The paper never cleanly defines whether the decoded sequence is MAP under the joint path posterior, per-timestep smoothed argmax, or Viterbi-like backtracking over particles.

The evaluation is visually persuasive but quantitatively thin. Most of the evidence is shown through figures and trajectories, not through precise quantitative summaries. There are no result tables summarizing exact means, standard deviations, confidence intervals, task counts, or statistical comparisons.

The computational cost and scaling behavior are not seriously analyzed. The method relies on particle filtering with K=250 particles during training... but the paper makes no attempt to characterize training or inference complexity as a function of sequence length T, number of modules N, or particle count K.

The novelty positioning is somewhat overstated relative to prior 'task inference' views of meta-learning. The framing that solving test tasks by inference is fundamentally different from prior meta-learning is too strong. There is already a line of work, especially in meta-RL and probabilistic meta-learning, that casts fast adaptation as inference over latent task variables rather than direct weight updates. One relevant example that appears missing from the bibliography is Meta reinforcement learning as task inference (Humplik et al., 2019).

The generalization claims are stronger than what the experiments establish. In Section 2.3 the authors argue that because the model learns sequencing rules, it 'automatically generalises to longer tasks without retraining,' supported by Figure 2f and Figure 3f. But these longer tasks are still generated by the exact same fixed-duration module grammar seen in training, merely concatenated for more timesteps. That is a much weaker notion of extrapolation than, for example, handling new duration statistics, insertions/deletions, noisy module reuse, or novel compositions with partial overlap.

Some figure references are mildly confusing, which hurts precision. On Page 7, the text says 'The history-dependent transition matrices, analogous to Figure 4c,' but it is clearly referring to Figure 2c.

The central theoretical framing is overstated, and key claims are not justified by the derivations presented. The paper claims SVM principles are valid only in Euclidean space, but does not provide proofs, only informal manipulations. KKT conditions are optimization conditions, not a geometric privilege exclusive to Euclidean spaces.

The mathematical derivation confuses coordinate transformation, metric choice, and existence of distinct class-specific spaces. The two classes are mapped by two different linear operators, so the data are no longer in one common transformed feature space, yet the paper proceeds as if a single linear SVM applies uniformly.

The margin formulas in the input space are presented as if they directly justify a new optimization problem, but the logic is incomplete. There is no proof that solving separate objectives is equivalent to the claimed transformed-space SVM, and the paper never specifies a single coherent prediction function derived from a single optimization objective.

The proposed SM algorithm appears to use test inputs during iterative relabeling, which makes the evaluation protocol problematic and risks transductive leakage. The method uses the full test input set at training/adaptation time, but is not framed as transductive learning and baselines do not receive analogous access to unlabeled test inputs.

The experimental setup is underspecified to the point that reproducibility and interpretation are both weak. The paper does not report essential details like hyperparameter selection, feature standardization, random seeds, class imbalance handling, or convergence thresholds.

The empirical gains are modest and not analyzed statistically. Many improvements are tiny (e.g., 0.002 absolute gain in accuracy), and there are no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

The baseline set is not convincing relative to the paper's own claims. The introduction cites multiple variance-aware or covariance-aware SVM variants, but none of those methods appear in the experiments.

The paper's positioning against prior work is too sweeping and insufficiently evidenced. It claims prior work has 'gaps in application of appropriate vector spaces and dimensional inconsistencies' but gives no concrete examples of which equations are dimensionally inconsistent.

The treatment of multi-class classification is speculative. Lemma 2.2 states an N-class problem yields N input spaces and N linear classifiers, but there is no multi-class method, derivation, or experiment beyond binary classification.

There are notation inconsistencies and mathematical sloppiness that make already-fragile arguments harder to follow, such as switching between Psi and psi, and never clearly stating the relationship between theta_Euclidean and theta_Input.

Some of the figures raise interpretability questions rather than strengthening the case. The ROC curves are fairly close across methods and some look piecewise coarse, yet the paper draws strong conclusions validating the lemmas from these results.

The paper conflates 'non-Euclidean space' in a broad geometric sense with standard vector spaces equipped with covariance-induced metrics, overstating the scope and potentially misleading readers into thinking it addresses general learning on non-Euclidean domains.

The core empirical conclusion is weaker than the rhetoric suggests, because the paper mainly shows robustness under perturbations of the independent variable N, not robustness of the underlying compute-optimal scaling claim itself. It does not probe robustness to the more consequential issues raised in the literature, such as experimental design, optimizer dependence, training horizon choices, data quality, or misspecification of the separable power-law form itself.

The 'best fit formula' in Section 2 is under-justified and somewhat ad hoc. The authors replace the attention multiplier 4 with 5 without giving a principled architectural reason for this choice, making it read like a reverse-engineered fit to reported numbers rather than a faithful reconstruction of the architecture.

The statistical evidence for 'no meaningful change' is not very strong, because the comparisons are largely visual and bootstrap-based without sharper hypothesis testing or practical-effect criteria. Overlap of error bars is not a strong statistical argument for equivalence, and the paper does not define a practical equivalence margin.

Some mathematical exposition is sloppy or internally inconsistent, which is avoidable in a paper whose main object is a fitted equation. There are notation inconsistencies between Sections 3 and Appendix C, alternating between N̂_i and Ñ_i, and between Â, α̂ without prior clean definition.

Section 3.3 states that α̂=10^{−0.46}⋅s^{−1} with R^2 > 0.999, but this is an empirical curve fit to fitted estimates, not a theorem. The paper would be stronger if it consistently distinguished exact algebraic consequences from empirical regressions on bootstrap outputs.

Equation (5) is not really an equation in the technical sense, it just states the heuristic '≈ 20'. The exposition would benefit from putting the derived formula (essentially Appendix Equations (16)-(17)) in the main text instead of presenting the heuristic as if it were the mathematical object of study.

The sensitivity analysis is interesting, but the perturbation ranges are only weakly tied to realistic sources of error, so the practical significance is murky. For example, the multiplicative perturbation sweeps c_m from 10^{-3} to 10^{3}, which is far beyond any plausible model-parameter miscount. The paper should be much clearer that this is a mathematical stress test rather than an empirical claim about realistic ambiguity.

The paper does not sufficiently engage with whether the observed robustness is partly a consequence of limited identifiability in the underlying fit. The paper interprets lack of movement under perturbations as evidence of stability, without seriously considering the alternative explanation that the model is simply weakly identified.

The contribution is somewhat incremental relative to existing Chinchilla replication and reconciliation work, and the paper’s positioning does not fully articulate what is fundamentally new. The paper uses existing Chinchilla data and existing fitting code, and its main results are re-fits plus synthetic perturbation studies.

The results figures are informative, but some of the paper’s main claims should have been supported by tables with explicit numerical comparisons rather than only plots. For a paper arguing 'no meaningful change,' a small results table quantifying effect sizes would be much more convincing than relying primarily on visual inspection of wide intervals.

There is no analogous table to Table 1 summarizing the actual downstream scaling-law fit outputs across the three interpretations, making it harder to audit the practical magnitude of the reported robustness.

There is some imprecision in how the paper connects its perturbations to real architectural counting conventions. Additive constants are motivated by inclusion or exclusion of embeddings, but embedding parameters are not truly an architecture-independent constant across arbitrary model families; they depend on vocabulary size and model dimension. The text sometimes speaks as if additive perturbations are a general abstraction of embedding inclusion/exclusion, which is too loose.

The paper’s practical recommendation is broader than what was actually validated. The conclusion says the work should give practitioners 'even greater confidence' in Chinchilla’s prescription, but at most the paper shows that under one family of published Chinchilla training runs, the fitted recommendation is not highly sensitive to several redefinitions of N. It does not validate Chinchilla across modern regimes with different data mixtures, optimizer choices, architectural families, or inference-aware objectives.

The dataset construction introduces a strong selection bias because the final sample is chosen via a text-based sentiment filter (VADER) rather than a sign-based emotional criterion, which may cause the benchmark to favor text-aligned emotional content.

The scale of the dataset is very small for the breadth of claims made, and the class support is thin enough that several benchmark conclusions feel overstated without uncertainty estimates or confidence intervals.

The annotation aggregation and reliability analysis are not strong enough for several labels, yet the paper proceeds as if the labels were equally stable across the board, conflating model failure with label instability.
The benchmark methodology is not sufficiently controlled to support strong conclusions about multimodal integration because different models use different prompting strategies.
Several evaluation details are underspecified or confusing, especially the metric definitions for 'wAcc' and 'wF1' which are never clearly specified.

The single-label emotion classification task discards important structure in the annotations, and the subset construction is too ad hoc without justification for why these transformations preserve the scientific target.
The qualitative grounding analysis is methodologically weak, relying on manually inspecting several randomly selected videos without a systematic annotation protocol or quantitative measure.

The results in Table 3 and Table 4 do not consistently support the paper's strongest interpretation that visual information contributes meaningfully, as caption-only is sometimes similar to or better than video+caption.

The paper does not adequately separate dataset contribution from benchmark contribution, and the latter is relatively weak because it lacks a sign-language-specific encoder baseline, pose/landmark baseline, or simple supervised classifier.

The literature positioning is thinner than it should be for a paper claiming a first benchmark in this area, lacking a broader discussion of work on emotionality and facial-expression modeling in sign language.
The paper raises an important conceptual issue, grammatical versus affective use of facial expressions, but never operationalizes it in the dataset or evaluation.
There are some presentation issues and overclaims, such as not explaining the verification protocol for cues and a typo.

The central theoretical positioning is stronger than what the main paper really establishes. The paper repeatedly leans on the theoretical grounding of Adjoint Matching, but the actual method used here departs from the clean setting in several important ways: a surrogate parameter flow built from φ, a scaled memoryless schedule with parameter κ, time-grid tilting, clipped losses, partial time-step supervision, and a regularization cost. The paper should be much more explicit about which parts are theory-backed and which parts are pragmatic stabilizers.

The joint parameter evolution is conceptually interesting, but its probabilistic meaning is underspecified and arguably shaky. The 'base' parameter flow is not learned from data and not derived from an actual joint process; it is constructed from a one-step terminal estimate. The paper never really clarifies what distribution over α is being represented along the path, why Gaussian initialization α0∼N(0,I) is sensible for PDE coefficient fields, or whether the induced joint process has any consistency guarantees beyond being useful as a regularizer.

There are mathematical and notation issues in the main method section that make careful verification harder than it should be. In Section 3.2, the sentence 'this can be achieved by directly learning the vector field v_{t,α}^R jointly with v_{t,α}^R' appears to repeat the same symbol and likely intends a joint state/parameter field. In Equation (3) and the surrounding text, gradients are written with respect to x̂, even though the augmented state is denoted X̂_t=(X_t^⊤,α_t^⊤)^⊤; that is a notational mismatch. Also, Equation (1) defines η_t=γ_t((β̇_t/β)γ_t−γ̇_t), but the numerator/denominator dependence is easy to misread and the notation is not carried consistently into later formulas.

The weak-residual construction is sensible, but the exact reward being optimized is not standardized across tasks, which makes cross-benchmark interpretation slippery. The appendix introduces task-specific normalizations: by mean permeability, mean modulus, local Helmholtz energy, or viscosity-weighted kinetic energy. Those choices are quite consequential. They affect the scale of the reward, the gradient magnitudes, and the reported 'relative residual' numbers. The paper should explain in the main text why these normalizations are the right ones, and how sensitive results are to them.

The evaluation protocol favors the proposed method in a way that is not fully disentangled. The reference set D_ref is defined as a synthetic clean dataset generated under the target PDE specification assumed during fine-tuning. Residuals and MMDs are then computed against this target-specification reference set. For misspecification settings, this means the evaluation is explicitly aligned with the fine-tuning objective rather than with the original observational data distribution. Claims about 'preserving the learned distribution' need more care, because otherwise one can trade off toward the assumed model class and call it an improvement even if one has drifted from the empirical distribution that motivated the pretraining.

Some baseline choices are useful, but the comparison landscape is still incomplete and occasionally framed too favorably. There is no direct comparison to simpler post-hoc alternatives such as optimizing α=φ(x_1) only at the endpoint and then performing gradient-based correction of the sample, or alternating sample correction with parameter inference without learning a full joint flow. The paper needs stronger evidence that the gains are not attainable with a simpler endpoint-parameterization approach. Also, the text in Appendix E.2 notes that all PDE settings deliberately introduce mismatch and that this 'naturally places [PBFM] at a disadvantage'.

The main-paper quantitative reporting is selective and occasionally hard to parse. The linear elasticity table is presented awkwardly: the table appears before the label 'Table 1' description on Page 9, and the text around it is easy to misread. More importantly, the main paper often presents 'representative configurations' rather than systematic best-vs-best or Pareto-front summaries. For example, Table 2 explicitly reports representative configs selected either by lowest weak residual or lowest MMD_x. That makes the comparison somewhat pliable because different methods may be highlighted under different selection criteria. A cleaner presentation would report Pareto fronts or matched operating points in the main paper, not just representative snapshots.

There is evidence of instability or possible reporting issues in the appendix tables, and the main text does not discuss them. The most glaring example is Table 12 on Helmholtz, where the last row reports for AM with λ_x=100M, λ_f=1, R_weak = 4.32 × 10^9 (± 1.43), while neighboring rows are around 10^0. This is either a typo or a severe instability, but the paper never flags it. Similarly, several tables show highly non-monotone behavior as λ_x increases, especially in Darcy (Table 10) where weak residual first improves and then worsens dramatically for large λ_x, while MMD remains tiny for some AM settings. Those patterns deserve explicit discussion, because they suggest the method is quite sensitive and the optimization story is less tidy than the main text implies.

The natural-image experiment is too thin to carry much weight as a cross-domain validation. There is one main prompt/class example in the body, no quantitative metric in the main text, and no clear ablation isolating whether the gain comes from the joint parameter pathway versus simply adding a hand-designed color transform family. So the cross-domain claim is more of a demonstration than a convincing validation.

The paper overstates preservation of diversity and sample-specific detail relative to the evidence shown. In Darcy, Figure 3(a) uses SSIM-based diversity on inferred parameter maps, and Figure 3(b) uses MMD_x versus residual under varying λ_f. These do show a trade-off, but they are limited proxies. For example, low MMD_x to the target reference set does not directly establish preservation of the base model's diversity; it only suggests closeness to one reference distribution. Likewise, preserving sample-specific detail is illustrated nicely in Figure 2, but only qualitatively and for a single seed. The presented evidence supports a softer, narrower statement, not the stronger one.
The submission lacks a dedicated Related Work section in the provided main paper text, which is part of the minimum required paper structure for this methodological study.

The central conceptual move is weaker than the paper suggests, and the novelty claim is overstated. The core mechanism is a penalty-based method with a binary, critic-dependent penalty instead of a scalar Lagrange multiplier, making the distinction from Lagrangian approaches less sharp than claimed.

The theoretical reformulation is not fully convincing, because it quietly changes the problem and then proves equivalence only under strong assumptions. Equation (2) replaces the original CMDP constraint with a stricter pointwise requirement, which means the proposed method is not actually solving the stated OSRL problem in general, but a stricter surrogate.

Theorem 1 is too narrow to justify the practical algorithm, and parts of the proof are sloppy. The theorem assumes the existence of a solution to Problem (2) and there is a large gap between the exact policy-dependent relabeled objective and the stochastic mini-batch procedure with approximate FQE.

Several mathematical definitions in the problem setup are imprecise or incorrect enough to undermine confidence. The value functions are defined with a shifted discounting convention dropping the immediate reward term, and there is a typo confusing Q_r and Q_c, which affects the exact meaning of the proposed constraints and theorem.

The safety guarantee is only as good as the cost critic, yet the main paper does not sufficiently quantify critic quality or calibration. There is no analysis of calibration, no threshold margin study, no estimate of false safe vs false unsafe classifications, and no comparison to softer relabeling rules.

The empirical claims are somewhat selective, and the headline statement of 'reliably enforces safety' is stronger than what Table 1 actually shows. CARL violates the cost threshold on some Safety-Gym tasks, and some baselines achieve substantially higher reward while remaining safe.

The comparison against baselines is incomplete for the paper’s strongest claims. The main paper does not include direct comparisons to simple penalty baselines that are closer to CARL than the chosen competitors, such as a fixed reward r-λc, a thresholded penalty variant using immediate cost, or a soft version of Equation (5).

The 'no additional hyperparameters' claim is too convenient. The method is quite sensitive to how the penalty is instantiated (e.g., using R_max vs V_max), so replacing λ with a thresholded penalty whose magnitude choice still matters a lot is sleight of hand.

The main empirical evidence for the stability story is underdeveloped. Figure 1 shows only one task, one backbone, and one setting, with no systematic ablation over M and K, no quantitative stability metric, and no results table showing whether M=K=1 is consistently better across tasks.

Some presentation and exposition issues make the paper harder to trust than necessary. There are multiple typographical and notation issues across Pages 2 to 4, and Figure 2 excludes the more challenging tasks where adaptation may fail, making the figure read a bit curated.

The paper occasionally over-interprets qualitative evidence. Figure 3 shows final policy outcomes in three tasks but does not establish that the method 'transforms unsafe dataset trajectories into safe ones' in any deep sense without quantifying coverage, distance to unsafe regions, or episode-level safety rate.

The practical scope is narrower than the framing suggests. The method assumes access to per-transition costs and hinges on reasonably learnable cost-to-go structure, but the introduction implies broad applicability to safety-critical domains like healthcare and autonomy where the binary relabeling rule may be brittle.

The novelty claim is overstated relative to what is actually introduced. The method itself is largely a composition of familiar ingredients: prototype or cache accumulation, attention-based lightweight adaptation, and a prior-adjusted entropy objective. The paper does not do enough to separate 'new setting' from 'new mechanism.'

Several of the paper's 'VLM-specific' failure-mode claims are not convincingly established as specific to VLMs rather than general imbalance effects. Figure 1(b.1) mainly shows classwise variability and alignment-level trends without a clean causal test that isolates text priors from the visual stream or from ordinary class difficulty. Figure 1(b.2) compares SAR on a VLM backbone versus a visual backbone, but this alone does not demonstrate that modality mismatch is the core reason for failure; there are many confounders between backbone families and adaptation dynamics.

In Equation (4), the update is described as 'via an EMA manner,' but the formula is not a standard EMA with a fixed momentum. Instead, it looks like a normalized running average indexed by N_{c,s}^{DP}. That is not merely terminology, it changes the adaptation dynamics materially.

In Equation (5), the notation is awkward and partly inconsistent. phi_c is written as a scalar but boldfaced, and the update counter N_{c,s}^{EP} is said to 'increase by phi_c at each step,' which means the counter is fractional. The semantics of 'counter' and the resulting normalization need to be defined much more carefully.

In Equation (6), the attention operator is underspecified. The text says 'RS is implemented by a cross-attention with shared hyper-class vectors,' yet the formula Attn([v_c,t_c], q_j)q_j + v_c does not define query, key, and value projections, nor whether the update sums over j or uses a single selected j. As written, the equation is not operationally complete.

In Equation (7), the CRA loss resembles a load-balancing surrogate, but the construction is difficult to verify because the pseudo-label counts and average activations are multiplied without a clear normalization or justification for why minimizing that dot product yields uniform expert usage. The connection to MoE load balancing is asserted more than derived.

The theoretical claims around BEM are much weaker than the paper suggests. Proposition 1 and Proposition 2 are stated as guarantees of rebalancing behavior, but the assumptions are too vague to support the strength of these claims. The split into C_head and C_tail is left abstract, and the propositions reason about expectations of logit gradients without specifying the underlying data distribution or confidence distribution. The propositions do not establish anything like optimization convergence, improved risk, or even monotone balancing on actual streams; they only state inequalities on expected gradients under assumptions that are not checkable from the main text. The theory currently reads more like suggestive intuition dressed up as a guarantee.

The definition of BEM itself in Equation (9) is not fully clear. The penalty term uses (1-hat{P})^beta, but hat{P} is not cleanly defined in the equation. It appears to be derived from the current prediction, yet the paper does not state whether it is the classwise softmax over z, the max-confidence scalar, or a detached pseudo-label distribution. This is not a cosmetic notation issue, because the gradient of L_BEM depends critically on whether that factor is treated as a differentiable function of z or as a constant weight.

The class prior pi is 'continually updated based on the current predicted pseudolabels,' which risks reinforcing early head-class bias. The paper claims BEM mitigates this, but does not explain why the self-updated prior does not simply drift toward the same dominant classes.

In Table 2, the ImageNet result for L-TTA is reported as 70.46 / 64.39, whereas nearly every baseline is in the mid-80s to high-80s for accuracy on the same row block. That is a dramatic drop, yet the row still contributes to a reported best overall average. This may be a typo, a different protocol, or a formatting issue, but as printed it is hard to reconcile with the surrounding numbers and should not be left ambiguous.

In Table 1, the dataset header changes from ImageNet-R at imb=10 to ImageNet-B at imb=20 and 50, while the text of the benchmark earlier describes ImageNet-A, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-S, and ImageNet-V2. This looks like a labeling inconsistency. It may be minor editorially, but it raises avoidable confusion about what was actually evaluated.

In Table 4, memory for WATT is listed as '1.54 x 71,' which is unusual formatting and not directly interpretable. Since this table is meant to support efficiency claims, the reported units and notation should be unambiguous.

The fairness of the long-tailed benchmark construction is not fully convincing. On Page 7, the paper says that datasets are manipulated by random sampling into an exponentially decayed class distribution, but 'if the calculated cardinality is less than the class cardinality itself, we simply keep that class unchanged.' This sentence is confusing, because a calculated target cardinality being less than the existing class size is precisely when one would expect subsampling. If this means some datasets remain only mildly imbalanced or partially modified, then the actual imbalance protocol may differ across datasets in a way that complicates comparison. Since the entire paper is built around synthetic long-tail generation, the protocol needs to be much more explicit in the main text.

The implementation details contain at least one likely typo with methodological implications. On Page 7, the paper states K = 0.3, even though K was introduced as the number of hyper-class vectors in Equation (6) and should therefore be an integer. Later, Figure 4(c) also studies 'vector number K' over values from 0.1 to 1, suggesting that the actual tuned quantity is probably a ratio rather than a count. This inconsistency matters because it obscures what architecture was actually instantiated.

Some of the claims drawn from the figures are stronger than what the figures really support. Figure 2(a) shows t-SNE plots comparing SCAP and L-TTA, but t-SNE is fragile and visually persuasive in ways that are not always reliable for quantitative conclusions. Saying that existing methods show 'severe degradation in tail-class representations' based on this panel is a bit too strong.

Figure 2(b) on macro-F1 versus imbalance ratio includes only a small subset of baselines. If this figure is used as core evidence of robustness, then either more methods should be shown or the claim should be narrowed.

The writing is understandable overall, but the exposition is rough in many local places. There are repeated grammatical errors, inconsistent naming, and notation drift. Examples include 'how summarizes how' on Page 5, switching between ImageNet-V and ImageNet-V2 or ImageNet-R/ImageNet-B in tables, 'attenticon' in Equation (7), and class/vector variable naming that changes meaning across sections. None of these individually kill the paper, but together they make the method harder to audit than it should be for a conference paper proposing multiple intertwined components.

The central claim is 'faithful reasoning,' but the paper mostly demonstrates better task performance and more legible rationales, not faithfulness in a strong scientific sense. The experimental section does not contain a dedicated faithfulness evaluation, such as perturbation tests, rationale-answer consistency checks, intervention studies, or human verification rates for the grounding trace.

The contribution of perceptual grounding is not cleanly isolated from ordinary domain adaptation and task supervision. The ablation does not separate confounded factors such as more supervision versus different supervision format, remote-sensing-specific task tuning versus grounding-specific supervision, and chain-of-thought structure versus explicit spatial evidence.

The GRPO formulation and reward design are underspecified, and in places mathematically inconsistent or at least sloppy enough to reduce confidence. The policy objective in Equation (3) omits the image and question conditioning variables, and the rewards in Table 3 are almost entirely final-answer rewards rather than rationale rewards, creating a mismatch between the method and the claim of refining faithfulness.

There is insufficient detail on several implementation choices required to assess stability and fairness: group size k, clipping parameter epsilon, KL coefficient beta, how partial correctness is operationalized for VQA/classification, how mAP reward is computed for free-form generative outputs in detection, and whether rewards are dense or sequence-terminal only.

The dataset construction pipeline's scientific reliability is not adequately audited in the main paper. The paper does not provide a manual audit of rationale correctness, diversity, or error modes, nor does it quantify how often generated rationales omit objects, inject unsupported statements, or simply paraphrase the provided answer and auxiliary signals.

Some reported empirical results are unusually large relative to baselines, but the paper does not do enough in the main text to rule out evaluation or protocol mismatches. The paper should proactively clarify whether all models were prompted identically, whether proprietary systems were allowed tool use, how outputs were parsed into boxes, and whether any task-specific post-processing was used for RSThinker but not for others.

Presentation quality is uneven, and there are many textual and formatting issues that obstruct technical confidence, such as malformed tags, corrupted outputs, wording errors (e.g., 'Syndrome' instead of 'Synthesis'), and inconsistent metric footers.

Several key methodological choices are deferred out of the main paper, leaving the main contribution under-specified. Critical details like object detection output serialization, box normalization convention, how duplicate boxes are handled during evaluation, and a concise formal schema for a valid grounded step are missing from the main text.

The paper's positioning against prior reasoning-with-RL work is somewhat overstated. The paper claims to be the first to propose such a framework for Earth Observation, but much of the training recipe (CoT-style SFT followed by GRPO-like RL) is a broader pattern in multimodal reasoning, blurring domain novelty with methodological novelty.

The paper does not include a dedicated Related Work section, and the provided text does not otherwise contain a substantive standalone discussion that situates the method against prior language-based audio retrieval, LLM augmentation, and cross-modal retrieval literature.

The paper's strongest claim, benchmark reliability through '100% TPR and 100% TNR,' is much less ironclad than the writing sometimes implies because these metrics are computed only on the authors' collected solution set, not on the full space of possible correct and incorrect programs.

The paper does not quantify how representative the collected incorrect solutions actually are, lacking a systematic analysis of whether these incorrect solutions cover diverse failure modes or are clustered around a few common mistakes.

The methodology around difficulty labeling is too heuristic, with underspecified calibration across contests that differ substantially in strength and format, and slightly inconsistent text about how problems are divided into levels.
The comparison to prior benchmarks is too rhetorical and not empirical enough, lacking direct head-to-head evidence on overlapping model sets, overlapping time windows, or matched subsets.

The experimental protocol is underdeveloped, omitting several choices in the main paper that affect fairness and interpretation, such as whether temperature differs by model family, how sampling parameters are set for Pass@N, whether system prompts or reasoning controls are standardized, whether compile-and-repair or retry logic is disallowed, and how special-judge tasks are handled.

There is a nontrivial issue with the interpretation of Pass@N in Table 3, as the paper does not clearly specify whether Pass@2 and Pass@4 are computed from independent samples under the standard unbiased estimator, or simply by empirical success over repeated runs.
The paper's interpretation of Table 4 overreaches because category difficulty is confounded with category composition, and the main paper's conclusions should not hinge on appendix-only nuance.

Appendix D reveals that some problems in AetherCode itself have 'authorization or copyright status currently unverifiable,' which is a significant issue for an open benchmark release and deserves more transparent treatment in the main paper.
There are several naming inconsistencies and typos, for example 'Aether-Code' vs. 'AetherCode,' 'Puss@4' on Page 7, and duplicated / inconsistent model names in Table 8 for the Claude series.
Example 2 on Pages 21 to 23 appears malformed in places, including a broken truth table for the OR operator and very messy example formatting.

The TPR/TNR formalization is incomplete as an evaluation model because it implicitly treats each collected solution as an equally informative i.i.d.-like sample of the correctness space, which is unlikely to hold in practice, and the paper should discuss that these are empirical rates on a curated pool, not unbiased estimates of some population-level verifier property.

Some claims of being 'the first' are too broad relative to the evidence in the paper, such as 'the first benchmark to systematically collect latest problems from premier programming competitions worldwide,' where the exact novelty boundary is not pinned down with enough care.
The paper is missing a Discussion or Conclusion section in the provided text, which is required by the stated minimum-structure check.
There are serious technical clarity/correctness concerns in the theorem/proof pipeline.
There are serious technical clarity/correctness concerns in the evaluation setup.

The headline theoretical claim depends on a strong and weakly justified approximation assumption, and the paper somewhat overstates what is actually proved. The dimension/Lipschitz independence only appears after assuming the 'well-approximated condition' in Equation (17), which essentially encodes the desired conclusion as an assumption. The empirical support for this assumption in the main paper is also not very convincing, as Figure 5 right does not establish that H whitens the local Hessian, and Figure 4 is a synthetic simulation rather than evidence from actual LLM training.

There is a notable derivational issue around the transition from the least-squares formulation to the implemented estimator. The paper claims that $(u^\top H^{-1}u)^{-1}$ is a scalar independent of iterates and can be absorbed into the learning rate, but it actually depends on the sampled direction u and varies from step to step. Replacing this random normalization factor by a constant changes the estimator, and the paper currently presents Equation (8) as if it follows directly from the optimization problem, which is not accurate.

The mathematical exposition contains several inconsistencies that make the proof chain harder to trust, including notation/indexing problems such as the use of $S_r$ vs $C_r$, unclear within-round indexing for $H_{r+1}$, identically written cases in Equation (32), an inverted communication iteration condition in Section F.4, and typos in Algorithm 2a and 2b in the appendix.

The Hessian-learning mechanism is much closer to an Adam-style second-moment accumulator than to an actual Hessian estimator, so some of the language in Section 4.2 is too strong. The update accumulates squared update magnitudes rather than estimating diagonal Hessian entries in a direct sense, and the paper repeatedly says it is 'learning global curvature' and 'approximating the diagonal Hessian' without clean mathematical justification.

The paper lacks a baseline that uses the same scalar-only framework with a generic adaptive diagonal accumulator but without the Hessian interpretation. Without this ablation, the gains cannot be properly isolated to specifically Hessian-informed perturbations versus generic adaptive rescaling.

The experimental comparison protocol in Table 2 is not presented in a symmetric way. It compares DeComFL at 'full convergence' against HiSo at the round where it first matches DeComFL's best accuracy, which is favorable to HiSo. A symmetric evaluation protocol (e.g., rounds to a common threshold, area-under-curve, or final best performance under equal communication budgets) would be more convincing.

There is a tension between the text and Table 3 regarding communication cost. The paper claims HiSo's communication cost is 'only a little higher than DeComFL on OPT-1.3B+QQP,' but the numbers are 96.67 KB for HiSo versus 43.95 KB for DeComFL, which is more than 2x higher, weakening the rhetoric.

The paper's empirical support for the claimed Hessian mechanism is thinner than it should be. The main-paper ablation (Figure 5 left) does not establish that the performance gain comes from better Hessian approximation rather than just a benign smoothing effect, and Figure 5 right is descriptive but indirect. The paper needs a stronger main-paper analysis tying the quality of H to performance to support the mechanistic claim.

The main theoretical claims are stronger than what the main paper really establishes. The abstract and contributions claim a rigorous proof that mode-seeking samplers create anti-alignment and thereby guarantee the effectiveness of negative extrapolation. In the main text, however, the core guarantee is heavily local and assumption-dependent. Equation (4) on Page 5 gives only a local Taylor expansion around θr, and Theorem 1 requires small ∥ε∥Hd, bounded preconditioned geometry, and favorable bias terms (η0,η1,cosφ). For diffusion and flow models, the key step is pushed into the appendix and relies on an additional curvature-density coupling assumption (A-MONO in Appendix B.7), which is not stated in the main paper when the universality claim is made.

There are several notation and exposition inconsistencies in the core technical sections, and they are not trivial cosmetic issues because they undermine confidence in a theory-heavy paper. A few examples: - In Equation (5) on Page 5, the sampler notation suddenly becomes qθr,n, whereas earlier the paper defines qθ,κ; that looks like an indexing error. - In Section 4 on Page 6, the text says “starting from a public checkpoint Gθs,” but throughout the method the base model should be Gθr. - On Page 9, the discussion of model quality refers to the condition ∥ε∥F being small, but the main theory is written in the Hd-geometry, ∥ε∥Hd. - The caption of Figure 4 on Page 7 appears broken: it says both w=−1 and w=0 correspond to θNeon=θ∗, which cannot be right and conflicts with the text around it.

The experimental story does not cleanly isolate how much of the gain comes from Neon itself versus post-hoc retuning of inference hyperparameters. This is especially clear in the autoregressive and IMM sections. On Page 7, the paper says evaluation jointly optimizes both merge weight w and CFG scale γ, and Figure 6 on Page 8 explicitly argues that joint tuning is “crucial.” But then the comparison that matters is not only base model vs base+Neon, it is also “base model with re-optimized γ” vs “Neon with re-optimized (w,γ)”, and similarly “self-trained checkpoint with re-optimized γ” vs Neon. The paper does not report this decomposition clearly enough. Since γ alone can strongly alter the precision-recall trade-off, some of the reported FID gain may be coming from retuning the sampler after weight modification rather than from the specific negative extrapolation principle.

The paper is missing a set of simple but important baselines that would help establish that the benefit is specific to the proposed degradation direction rather than generic weight extrapolation. For example, I would have liked to see comparisons to: - extrapolating along a standard late-training checkpoint direction from the original training run, - interpolation / extrapolation between neighboring checkpoints without any synthetic self-training, - a generic one-step “negative learning rate” update along some unrelated or random synthetic batch direction, - EMA/SWA-style or checkpoint-averaging baselines where applicable. Right now, the evidence shows that “this particular direction found by short self-training can be useful,” but it does not fully rule out the simpler explanation that many mildly improving extrapolation directions exist in these pretrained generators.

The empirical results are broad, but the paper is thin on robustness statistics. Almost every claim is reported as a best FID after searching over w and sometimes γ, yet there are no error bars, confidence intervals, or seed-to-seed variability estimates in the main paper. This especially matters for claims like “works effectively with as few as 1k synthetic samples” and for the tiny compute-overhead regime, where the outcome could be sensitive to noise in fine-tuning or evaluation. Figure 3 and Figure 5 present smooth curves with multiple settings, but without any uncertainty it is hard to judge how stable the gains really are.

Some of the strongest claims in the contribution list are supported by relatively narrow evidence. The transfer claim [C5] is based mainly on Figure 8 on Page 9, where one target model, EDM-VP on CIFAR-10, is improved using synthetic data from two other architectures. That is an interesting proof of concept, but “the degradation signal is transferable” reads broader than what is actually demonstrated in the main paper. Similarly, the claim that Neon does not require a near-optimal base model, based on Figure 9, is suggestive, but still only shown for one architecture and one dataset.

The comparison framing in Table A.1 should be read carefully. The table is helpful, but it also mixes very different model families, different numbers of function evaluations, and different kinds of post-hoc methods. That is fine for context, but some of the prose around it occasionally drifts toward a stronger “state-of-the-art” framing than the table fully justifies across all settings. For instance, on FFHQ-64 and ImageNet-512 the paper is clearly competitive rather than best. I do not object to the ImageNet-256 claim, but the broader tone could be more measured.

The theorem-to-practice bridge is still somewhat loose. In the theory, the synthetic distribution is frozen as qθr,κ and the analysis is local in a population-risk sense. In practice, the method uses finite synthetic datasets, original training recipes, learning-rate schedules, and checkpoint selection after tuning. The appendix does discuss finite-sample effects, but from the main paper alone it is still not obvious when the practical recipe should fail, beyond the generic statement about diversity-seeking samplers. I would have liked a more explicit discussion of failure modes in the main text, especially since Figure 3 already hints at non-monotonic behavior in |S| and training budget.

The claimed theoretical framing around “asymmetry-aware embeddings” is much weaker than the paper suggests, and in its current form it is close to a rephrasing of low-rank matrix factorization rather than a substantive theory. Definition 1 is extremely permissive, the “≈ 0” is undefined, and the definition does not characterize anything specific to the proposed representation nor show that the learned embedding will preserve asymmetry after subsequent projection and encoder updates.

The dynamic asymmetry argument for Sinkhorn normalization is under-justified, both mathematically and empirically. Column normalization imposes marginal constraints on the attention matrix, but that does not by itself imply that A_{i,j} now captures the “complete neighborhood structure” of j. The empirical support is also thin; Table 6 shows Sinkhorn helps but does not isolate why, and Figure 8 raises the question that Sinkhorn may just be acting as a regularizer/anti-collapse effect rather than modeling dynamic asymmetry.

A key part of the method, namely the actual training objective and optimization protocol, is underspecified in the main paper. The main text describes the architecture and decoding procedure, but does not clearly state the learning objective (e.g., REINFORCE, rollout baseline, imitation, etc.), which strongly affects performance, stability, and reproducibility.

There are nontrivial mathematical and algorithmic clarity issues in the formulation. Equation (6) has a parenthesis mismatch and Sim() is left abstract. Algorithm 2 does not specify how masking of visited/infeasible nodes is handled in Sinkhorn normalization, nor does it address numerical stability for exponentiating scores. The proof-like discussion around Equations (3)-(5) only shows reconstruction before the learned projection layer, blurring the distinction.

The novelty is somewhat incremental relative to what is actually implemented. Strip away the rhetoric, and the method is “initialize node features using a truncated SVD of the asymmetric distance matrix, then replace softmax with Sinkhorn in a MatNet-style attention module,” which is a reasonable combination but not a major conceptual leap.

Some experimental comparisons are less clean than they first appear. In Table 1, many baselines are retrained under the authors’ setup with notable architecture changes (e.g., ELG adapted for asymmetry) and z-score normalization chosen by the authors, making the comparison depend heavily on a common reimplementation pipeline. There is also nomenclature sloppiness (e.g., “ReLU+” vs. ReLD).

The choice of the truncation rank k is not convincingly justified, and the justification that is given is somewhat concerning methodologically. The rank appears to be selected based on observed OOD test behavior rather than a principled criterion relating rank to instance size, asymmetry level, or downstream task difficulty.

The scalability story is not fully convincing for realistic asymmetric distance matrices. The method assumes access to the full n x n distance matrix and performs truncated SVD on it, which is workable at n <= 1000 but the asymptotic memory footprint remains quadratic in n, and there is no discussion of sparse, streaming, or partial-matrix variants.

The empirical section is broad but not always as decisive as the narrative suggests, especially with respect to classical solvers and real-world baselines. For the multi-task benchmark in Table 2, the average gap improvement is modest and the paper does not report variance or significance. On real-world data in Table 3, the baseline set is relatively narrow and partly inherited from another paper rather than re-run under matched settings.

Presentation quality is mixed despite generally readable prose. There are quite a few typos, notation inconsistencies, and overclaims (e.g., “ReLU+” vs. ReLD, “Runtime Ananlysis”, and text claiming the model “theoretically captures” something only heuristically supported). Some figure-based analyses are visually suggestive but not especially rigorous (e.g., Figure 2 reports final gap bars without uncertainty or matched compute).
Algorithm 1 on Page 6 references an update described as 'Eq. (4)', but Eq. (4) does not actually appear in the main paper, making the operative algorithmic object unclear in the main text.
Theorem 7 on Page 7 is stated for 'Algorithm 4 with Algorithm 2 as PosteriorUpdate,' but Algorithm 4 is only in the appendix, not the main paper, deferring the operative algorithmic object.

There is a nontrivial mismatch between the headline claim in the abstract ('Dig-DEC is always no larger than optimistic DEC') and the theorem actually stated in the main paper (Theorem 13), which only shows an additive-η comparison.

In Eq. (8) on Page 7, the definition of Dig-DEC first writes max over ν∈Δ(Φ), and then in the next line rewrites the objective with max over ν∈Δ(Ψ), creating ambiguity about the domain of the central world distribution ν.
Definition 9 on Page 8 ends with 'M∈M^3', which appears to be a typo affecting readability in a section defining Bellman completeness.

The assumptions for the hybrid setting (Assumption 2 and Assumption 3) are hard to parse from the main text alone, and the figure (Figure 1) that helps understand Assumption 2 is in the appendix rather than the main paper.

The formatting of Table 1 on Page 9 and Table 2 on Page 10 is bad enough that several regret expressions appear mangled (e.g., T^{5/3}, T^{1/9}, T^{3/3}), which materially hinders checking which rates are actually proved.

The experimental or illustrative validation is fairly minimal relative to the boldness of some claims, with no computational experiment, numerical study, or worked small-scale example in the main paper demonstrating how the Dig-DEC-driven policy differs behaviorally from optimistic E2D.

The mathematical role of the estimator terms is not always as transparent as it should be, such as in Theorem 7 where the connection between the estimation divergence and the aggregated estimators is hard to follow because objects are postponed.

Assumption 6 on Page 8 is rather intricate, involving ξ_h, T_M, and a quadratic dominance condition, but the paper gives limited intuition for why this assumption is the right one and in what sense it is close to standard Bellman completeness.

The computational status of the algorithm is largely abstracted away, with Eq. (3) requiring solving a minimax problem over Δ(Π) and Δ(Ψ), and the paper giving little guidance about whether this is purely existential, oracle-based, or reducible.

The comparison to prior work blends together two distinct contributions (the new complexity notion and the improved estimation procedure), and the paper should separate these more cleanly so readers do not over-credit Dig-DEC itself for improvements from better control of Est.

The main mathematical development is not presented with enough rigor or clarity in the main paper, and some equations appear inconsistent or under-specified. Specifically, the derivation from Equation (2) to Equation (4) is too compressed and requires a careful change-of-variables argument that is missing.
There is notation drift and inconsistency in the appendix proof of Equation (4), alternating between different notations for X_t, which makes several lines difficult to verify.
In Equation (5) on Page 4, the estimator includes s_θ^p and s_φ^q, but the third term suddenly uses s_0^p, which looks like a typo for s_θ^p and makes the core estimator ambiguous.

The pseudocode in Algorithms 1 to 3 contains multiple suspicious variable mismatches. In Algorithm 2, line 6 defines X~ although the loop is over components of Y_t, and line 7 mixes inconsistent variable notations in the same estimator.
Algorithm 3 has a malformed term (1/N(s^{θ(t)}-1)) that seems intended to be (1/N(e^{σ̄(t)}-1)), matching the discussion on Page 5 and Appendix A.2.

The theoretical claim of consistency is relegated to the appendix and depends on strong assumptions (bounded score ratios with constants C1, C2) that are not well interrogated in the main paper, particularly the lower bound C1>0 on score ratios in sparse high-dimensional discrete spaces.
